title: Forsee Power unveils ZEN 8 LFP battery, setting a new benchmark for electric off-highway machinery - Batteries News
content:
Forsee Power unveils ZEN 8 LFP battery, setting a new benchmark for electric off-highway machinery
Paris, November 18, 2026 – 5:45 p.m. CET – Forsee Power (FR0014005SB3 – ALFOR), an expert in smart battery systems for commercial and industrial electric vehicles, announces the launch of its next-generation ZEN 8, a compact lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery designed to accelerate the electrification of urban cleaning equipment, commercial utility vehicles, construction machinery and agricultural vehicles. With over 245 Wh/L energy density, the new European-made LFP battery combines high performance, simplified integration and competitive economics to accelerate the electrification of compact construction equipment.
Powered by next-generation 173 Ah LFP cells, for 45V nominal module voltage, the next-generation ZEN 8 matches its NMC predecessor’s energy capacity, voltage range and improves its performance and cycle-life targets. Its optimized thermal architecture eliminates the need for liquid cooling, simplifies vehicle integration and reduces system complexity. Supporting demanding daily operations with a targeted 0.7C fast-charging rate, it combines high energy density, LFP robustness advantages and competitive pricing to enable cost-effective solutions and rapid large-scale industrial deployment.
The new ZEN 8 LFP is ideal for compact electric street sweepers, supporting from 50 kWh to 130 kWh targeting 8 hours of operation, as well as compact non-road machinery: low-tonnage excavators, loaders, telehandlers, tractors, others. All those applications are operating in urban, construction, waste management and agricultural environments where low noise, zero emissions, reduced ownership cost and improved operational efficiency are non-negotiable.
Designed as a drop-in replacement for the existing ZEN 8 NMC battery, the new generation maintains the same external dimensions and mounting points, ensuring full mechanical compatibility.
The next-generation ZEN 8 enables existing customers to transition to LFP technology without vehicle redesign, reducing engineering efforts, development costs and time to market.
Manufactured in Europe, the ZEN 8 LFP reinforces Forsee Power’s commitment to strengthening the European battery value chain and supporting local industrial capabilities. Its European manufacturing footprint (France) also positions the product to support OEMs preparing for evolving European industrial and local-content requirements, including those under discussion in the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). The battery is designed to comply with the applicable requirements of the EU Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, including CE marking and Battery Passport obligations.
Christophe Gurtner,
Chairman and CEO of Forsee Power, commented:
With the new ZEN 8 LFP, we are combining exceptional LFP energy density, competitive pricing and European manufacturing in a solution designed for rapid industrial deployment.
”We are giving OEMs a simpler, more competitive way to electrify compact machinery while preparing for Europe’s evolving regulatory requirements”

content:
Ford Trucks and Circulor advance Battery Passport readiness for electric heavy commercial vehicles
Electrification is expanding beyond passenger cars and light commercial vehicles into the heavy-duty transport sector. While electric trucks still represent a relatively small share of the European market, adoption is accelerating.
Ford Trucks is advancing its electric mobility portfolio with the F-LINE E, its fully electric heavy commercial vehicle developed and manufactured by Ford Otosan. Presented as a key part of the Ford Trucks product portfolio at IAA Transportation 2026, the F-LINE E offers up to 392 kWh of battery capacity and a range of up to 300 kilometres, supporting regional distribution and urban operations.
As electric heavy commercial vehicles enter the market, manufacturers must also prepare for new regulatory and data-management requirements. From 18 February 2027, Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 will require each electric vehicle battery, each light means of transport battery and each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh that is placed on the EU market or put into service to have a Battery Passport.
The responsibility for creating and maintaining the Battery Passport lies with the economic operator placing the finished battery on the EU market. The passport will be linked to the battery through a QR code and will provide structured access to information concerning battery identification, technical characteristics, performance, durability, sustainability, circularity, repair, reuse and recycling. Access rights will vary depending on the type of information and the stakeholder requesting access.
To prepare for these requirements, Ford Otosan is working with Circulor to establish the supply chain data foundation required for compliant and reliable Battery Passports for Ford Trucks’ electric vehicle batteries.
The project begins with a structured mapping of the battery supply chain using supplier-declared data. This initial phase enables Ford Otosan to establish visibility across its supplier network and to create a traceable baseline covering the origin, processing and chain of custody of materials used throughout the battery value chain.
Due diligence requirements cannot be addressed through a single uniform approach. Different materials, suppliers and production locations may carry different levels of environmental, regulatory and supply chain risk. Supplier-declared information therefore provides the initial foundation, while higher-risk materials and supply chain connections may require additional documentation, evidence and independent assurance.
Using Circulor’s platform, Ford Otosan can request, collect and maintain supporting evidence for relevant supply chain declarations. Circulor’s tiered Trust and Assurance approach allows the level of verification to be adjusted according to the risk associated with individual materials, facilities and supply chain relationships. This helps Ford Otosan strengthen assurance progressively without having to redesign or restart the programme when supply chain risks or regulatory expectations change.
This supply chain data forms part of the foundation required for an accurate and compliant Battery Passport. The passport is designed as a dynamic digital record linked to the physical battery, allowing relevant information to remain accessible and updated throughout the battery’s lifecycle. The EU framework also establishes differentiated access rights so that public, restricted and commercially sensitive information can be managed appropriately.
At the scale of a heavy commercial vehicle programme, this requires the coordination of data across multiple battery configurations, vehicle models, suppliers and lifecycle participants. The collaboration between Ford Otosan and Circulor is intended to create the digital and organisational foundation needed to manage this complexity.
The project demonstrates how regulatory readiness, supply chain transparency and digital product information are becoming integral parts of the transition to electric heavy-duty transport. Passenger vehicles and heavy commercial vehicles have different duty cycles, battery configurations and supply chains, but they share a growing requirement for reliable and accessible information about the origin, composition, performance and lifecycle of their batteries.
Through this collaboration, Ford Otosan and Circulor are taking a practical step towards Battery Passport readiness and greater transparency across the electric heavy commercial vehicle value chain.

title: GMG Signs Service Agreement with the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre to Manufacture G⁠®CELLS in the UK - Batteries News
content:
GMG Signs Service Agreement with the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre to Manufacture G⁠®CELLS in the UK
BRISBANE, QUEENSLAND, AUSTRALIA – Graphene Manufacturing Group Ltd. (TSXV: GMG) (OTCQX: GMGMF) (“GMG” or the “Company“) is pleased to announce that it has signed an initial service agreement with the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre (“UKBIC“), the United Kingdom’s national battery manufacturing development facility located in Coventry, England, to carry out cell manufacturing of GMG’s next generation fast charging graphene battery cells (“G⁠®CELLS“).
Under the service agreement, the battery materials for the G⁠®CELLS will be developed, manufactured and supplied by GMG from its Battery Development Centre (“BDC“) in Richlands, Brisbane, Australia. The cells will then be manufactured and formed by UKBIC at its facility in Coventry. UKBIC will initially manufacture pouch cell format 1 G⁠®CELLS, as seen in Figure 1.
The UKBIC agreement adds a second international cell manufacturing partner to GMG’s battery program. GMG will continue to use the Battery Innovation Center of Indiana (“BIC Indiana“) in the United States of America, together with its own BDC in Brisbane, to make G⁠®CELLS. Having cell production capability across Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom is expected to increase GMG’s overall cell production capacity, allow additional cell formats to be developed in parallel, and provide sample cells closer to potential customers in Europe and the United Kingdom.
Consistent with GMG’s approach with BIC Indiana, GMG will pay for services rendered by UKBIC and retain all intellectual property of the G⁠®CELLS development work. Using UKBIC’s existing industrial-scale equipment allows GMG to progress cell scale-up and process development while deferring the capital expenditure of building its own large-format cell manufacturing capacity until the technology is further de-risked.
Sean Gilgunn,
Managing Director of UKBIC
commented:
UKBIC was established to help battery innovators bridge the gap between promising laboratory and pilot results and industrial-scale manufacturing.
”We’re pleased to be applying our production lines, process engineering and formation capability to build cells using GMG’s materials. Partnerships like this demonstrate the role UKBIC plays in supporting international battery developers to scale up, and in strengthening the battery manufacturing ecosystem in the United Kingdom.”
Craig Nicol,
Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director of GMG, commented:
Signing with UKBIC is an important step in scaling G⁠®CELLS to larger cell formats.
”Our materials will continue to be made by GMG at our Battery Development Centre in Richlands, and UKBIC will make and form the cells in Coventry. This sits alongside our ongoing work with BIC Indiana and our own cell production in Brisbane – so rather than replacing existing capabilities, it expands our manufacturing capacity and the number of formats we can deliver to customers for testing. Importantly, it also gives us a manufacturing presence in the United Kingdom and Europe, where we see strong interest in fast charging, long life battery technology. I would like to thank Sean and the UKBIC team for their support.”
Bob Galyen,
GMG Director and former Chief Technology Officer of CATL, commented:
Moving a new cell chemistry from small pouch cells into larger formats is where many battery technologies are truly tested, and it is the right next step for G⁠®CELLS following the cycle life and energy efficiency results generated at BIC Indiana.
”UKBIC has industrial-scale equipment covering electrode manufacturing, pouch and cylindrical cell assembly, and formation, ageing and testing – exactly what is needed to learn how the GMG materials behave at production-relevant scale. Having two experienced cell manufacturing partners in BIC Indiana and UKBIC, supplied with materials from GMG’s own Battery Development Centre, gives the team more opportunities to iterate on cell design and process, which is how robust, manufacturable cells are developed.”
Jack Perkowski,
Chairman of GMG, commented:
The Board’s strategy has always been to scale G⁠®CELLS through world-class partners rather than committing large amounts of capital to manufacturing plants before the technology is fully de-risked.
”UKBIC is one of the leading national battery scale-up facilities in the world, and adding it alongside BIC Indiana gives GMG two established cell manufacturing partners on two continents, supplied with materials made by GMG in Australia. This is a capital-efficient path toward commercial production and, over time, toward our longer-term goal of licensing the technology and supplying GMG materials to battery manufacturers globally. The Board will continue to support management as they execute on this next phase.”

title: onsemi's EliteSiC M4 Pushes Power Density Higher as Energy Demands Grow - Batteries News
content:
onsemi’s EliteSiC M4 Pushes Power Density Higher as Energy Demands Grow
Fourth-generation silicon carbide platform based on a trench architecture reduces losses while enabling more compact power systems across AI, EV and energy applications
onsemi introduced EliteSiC™ M4, its fourth-generation silicon carbide platform built on a trench architecture, delivering up to 30% higher power density and 35% lower losses compared with the previous generation. By advancing conduction and switching performance, EliteSiC M4 enables more efficient, power-dense systems for AI data centers, electric vehicles and energy infrastructure.
News Highlights:
EliteSiC™ M4 delivers higher power density and lower losses enabling customers to increase performance and efficiency while optimizing system size and managing cooling requirements
Extends onsemi’s proven SiC leadership, building on more than 16 billion miles of real-world operation
EliteSiC™ M4 750 V automotive traction bare die available now, with additional voltage options up to 1200 V expected in 2027
Scottsdale, Ariz. – Nov. 10, 2026 –
onsemi (Nasdaq: ON) today introduced EliteSiC™ M4, its fourth-generation silicon carbide (SiC) platform built on a trench architecture and designed to set a new performance benchmark for next-generation power systems. With industry-leading conduction and switching performance, EliteSiC M4 gives customers greater design freedom to increase power density and efficiency up to 30% and lower losses by 35%, enabling more efficient, power-dense systems across EVs, AI data center and industrial applications.
Achyut Shah
, Group President of the Power Solutions Group at onsemi, said:
Power requirements are rising faster than the physical infrastructure around them.
”The next generation of power systems will require the ability to deliver more power, more efficiently and in less space. With more than 16 billion miles of proven silicon carbide operation in vehicles around the world, EliteSiC M4 is combining that foundation of reliability with the performance customers need to rethink the balance among power, efficiency, size and cost.”
Delivering More Power Within Real-World Constraints
The growth of AI, electrification and energy infrastructure is creating a common challenge for power-system designers – delivering significantly more power without proportional increases in size, energy losses, and cooling requirements. EliteSiC M4 addresses that challenge by expanding the power and efficiency available within existing system constraints, giving customers greater flexibility to scale AI infrastructure, electric vehicles and industrial systems.
Across its key markets, EliteSiC M4 translates these technology advances into distinct system-level benefits:
AI Data Centers: Scaling compute without scaling power infrastructure at the same rate.
Higher-density power conversion helps data centers get more compute from every megawatt, maximizing capacity while reducing the supporting infrastructure required per unit of compute
Electric Vehicles: Getting more performance from the electric drivetrain.
More compact, efficient traction inverters can help automakers improve vehicle range
Energy Infrastructure: Making more of every unit of energy.
More efficient, higher-density power conversion helps solar, energy storage and other high-voltage systems reduce conversion losses
Harald Hartel
, Vice President, BU eMotor Controls at Schaeffler AG, said:
As vehicle power levels increase, traction-inverter design becomes a tighter balancing act between efficiency, thermal performance, power density and reliability,
“Higher efficiency and power density can give us greater flexibility to optimize the traction inverter for range, thermal performance and packaging, which are increasingly important as electrified powertrains become more demanding.”
A New Architecture for Higher Power Density and Efficiency
EliteSiC M4 improves conduction and switching performance without compromising reliability. Key improvements over the previous generation include:
Improvement in specific on-resistance (RSP):
Reduces specific RSP between 20% – 50%, while enabling faster switching
Lower switching losses:
Improves switching figures of merit by 67% in hard-switching and 50% in soft-switching, supporting compact power-supply designs
Broad packaging flexibility:
Designed to support existing packages, including top-side-cooled surface-mount packages and high-power modules
Ruggedness for demanding applications:
The platform is also designed for demanding operating environments, with qualification supporting temperatures of 185°C and above, enabling use in high-voltage automotive and space applications
Availability
The EliteSiC M4 750 V bare die for automotive traction inverters is available now. Additional product offerings for a range of voltages up to 1200 V are expected to be available beginning in 2027.

title: Sila Inks Long-Term Offtake Deal with Panasonic Energy to Power Domestic Battery Production - Batteries News

Sila Inks Long-Term Offtake Deal with Panasonic Energy to Power Domestic Battery Production
Agreement to deliver Sila’s Titan Silicon® Si/C anode to Panasonic’s U.S. manufacturing sites, fortifying domestic battery supply chain resilience and advanced technology capabilities.
ALAMEDA, CA — November 18, 2026 — Sila, a leading battery technology and materials company, today announced a commercial offtake agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America. The multi-year agreement is part of a long-term commercial relationship with the potential for over $1 billion of offtake over time. Sila will supply its proprietary Titan Silicon silicon-carbon (Si/C) anode material from its Moses Lake, Washington plant to power Panasonic battery cells. The partnership is also expected to support significant manufacturing and construction job creation in the United States. With Sila’s U.S.-based anode production underpinned by proprietary American technology and know-how, Panasonic and its OEM customers gain a clearer path toward a more secure, resilient, and sustainable domestic supply chain.
Gene Berdichevsky,
Co-founder and CEO of Sila, said:
This offtake agreement is a major commercial milestone for Sila, a signal that our Moses Lake plant will be ready to supply high-performance materials for our key strategic customers once qualified, and expand as needed,
“Partnering with a global industry leader like Panasonic validates our technology, ensuring anodes invented and manufactured in the U.S. are integrated into American-built cells to power critical industries for years to come.”
The agreement marks a significant step toward strengthening U.S. technological competitiveness and industrial resilience by manufacturing next-generation silicon-carbon anode materials here in the United States. Sila and Panasonic will also collaborate on intellectual property to further strengthen and develop their partnership.
Yasuaki Takamoto
, CEO, Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America, said:
Sila’s rapid progress at Moses Lake—from breaking ground to production—has been exceptional,
“Their technical leadership makes them a trusted partner as we work together toward meeting our highest quality and performance standards. This collaboration evidences Panasonic’s commitment to U.S. manufacturing while contributing to a more resilient battery supply chain in North America.”
The contract announced today follows Sila’s recent $1.4 billion loan commitment from the U.S. Department of Defense’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC). Securing strong commercial offtake agreements represents a key milestone and a natural next step toward demonstrating Sila’s execution and commercial readiness across the business. It also results in an estimated additional 500 manufacturing and construction jobs at Sila’s plant in Moses Lake, Washington, as the company scales production to meet volume requirements for this agreement and other commercial commitments.
Sila’s Moses Lake silicon-carbon anode manufacturing facility is expected to play a pivotal role in strengthening domestic battery manufacturing and securing key energy supply chains. By scaling proprietary Titan Silicon Si/C anode production locally, the facility reinforces U.S. manufacturing leadership, fosters regional high-tech job creation, and lays the foundation of a secure, competitive battery supply chain in North America for global electric vehicle, AI, and critical technology markets.

title: Ford Ships First Battery Cells from Michigan Plant for Fathom Electric Truck; Key Milestone for Ford Energy - Batteries News
content:
Ford Ships First Battery Cells from Michigan Plant for Fathom Electric Truck; Key Milestone for Ford Energy
The first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells are rolling off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan and headed to Louisville Assembly Plant to power Ford Fathom prototypes. With this milestone, Ford is now in the
battery business
and will be the first to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer automotive use.
The shipment caps years of work by the team that designed, built, and launched the plant on schedule. Ford now delivers cells at a plant it owns and operates, building expertise to support more affordable electric vehicles (EVs) and Ford Energy’s battery energy storage business in Kentucky.
Why Start with LFP Prismatic for Fathom?
When Alan Clarke, vice president, Advanced Development Projects, first joined the development team that created the Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, he issued a clear challenge: find an efficient LFP prismatic battery. The goal was to make EVs significantly more affordable.
We talked to battery companies around the world. We wanted a technology that was proven in the field, ready to manufacture at scale, and suited to what we were building. That led us to the world’s leading battery manufacturer, CATL, whose batteries power
30 million vehicles
across the globe.
A battery is one of the biggest contributors to an EV’s cost and weight. So, we asked: How do we get more out of the battery without simply adding more cells? Our answer was efficiency over excess.
LFP chemistry uses no nickel or cobalt, which helps hold down costs. It also holds up over years of charging and use. That durability is valuable as we give customers ways to use their battery beyond driving. For example,
AC bidirectional power
lets a vehicle receive electricity from a properly equipped home and supply power back to it.
We engineered Fathom for efficiency, too, right-sizing the battery and putting every electron and part to work.
Making the battery pack part of the vehicle structure is a key example. Rather than simply housing the battery pack within the vehicle, we designed it to serve as a structural component. We chose prismatic, or rectangular, cells because they fit directly into the chassis and cut structural costs.
We also combined electrical and sensing connections into a flexible circuit board and integrated compact power electronics into the pack. This architecture helps enable the new
Universal EV Production System
Our rule: The best part is no part, and the second-best part is one that serves multiple purposes. Fewer parts mean less weight and simpler manufacturing. Those details matter because they bring us closer to our goal: delivering an EV with the performance customers expect at a price that convinces drivers of gas-powered vehicles to make the switch.
Delivering with Quality at Scale
Making a battery cell is one thing. Delivering high-quality cells consistently, at the required scale and pace, is another.
The BlueOval Battery Park Michigan assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.
That pace helps drive down battery costs, and the facility has capacity for more. But speed must go hand in hand with quality.
Employees use AI-powered image recognition and other tools to spot defects during production. Our goal is to make defective cells so rare that we track their frequency per billion cells rather than per million.
What Comes Next?
The battery packs on their way to Louisville Assembly Plant are an important first step. They’ll help power Fathom prototypes and inform every phase of ongoing development. Next, we plan to have the battery pack plant up and running in Marshall in 2027 ahead of launch.
The knowledge we’re building in Michigan is already informing Ford Energy’s preparations for battery energy storage production in Glendale, Kentucky. The applications, customers, and products will be different, but the design expertise, controls, and manufacturing experience apply to both businesses.

title: SPRIND invests in battery recycler cylib - Batteries News
content:
SPRIND invests in battery recycler cylib
The goal: a closed loop for battery materials in Europe.
The foundation is a process developed at RWTH Aachen University that selectively recovers all raw materials from batteries.
Proof that it works comes from a Porsche AG pilot project in which cylib was among the partners supplying recycled lithium for cathode production: For the first time, the project produced battery cells with cathode active material made from 100% recycled raw materials.
Aachen, Germany, 17 November 2026.
SPRIND, Germany’s Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation, is taking a stake in Aachen-based battery recycling company cylib. The logic is simple: Europe has little access of its own to the raw materials that are critical for battery production, while the number of end-of-life EV batteries grows every year. cylib is working to keep these critical raw materials in a closed loop, from the end-of-life battery back into the value chain. SPRIND is now helping the company develop its technology further and scale it to industrial maturity.
“Our technology was born in research, and at cylib we have developed it to the threshold of industrialization,” says Dr. Lilian Schwich, co-CEO and co-founder of cylib. “With SPRIND, we gain a partner that understands how important technological innovation is for critical value chains and what it takes to bring it to market.”
Lithium first
The process is based on research at RWTH Aachen University. Early recycling processes focused on nickel and cobalt. Lithium was recovered only at the end of the process chain or was lost in the slag. At cylib, lithium comes first: The water-based OLiC process (Optimized Lithium and Graphite Recovery) extracts lithium in the very first steps from black mass, the powder produced by mechanically processing end-of-life batteries. A recent review in the journal Waste Management, co-authored by cylib CTO Dr. Tobias Elwert, shows that this approach can increase overall yields while also offering cost advantages. This matters for regulation as well: The EU Battery Regulation requires 80% of the lithium in waste batteries to be recovered by the end of 2031.
The pilot project involving cylib, Porsche AG and other partners shows that the process works in practice. As Porsche announced in September, the project produced cathode active material from 100% recycled raw materials for the first time, recovered from Porsche’s own high-voltage batteries. The cells made from this material are now being tested against Porsche’s stringent quality requirements.
Why SPRIND is investing
Olav Carlsen
, innovation manager at SPRIND, says:
Breakthrough innovations don’t only happen in the lab. They also happen where a technology makes a new market possible,
“cylib has the technological foundation to create a large-scale industrial market for battery materials that remain in circulation in Europe. That strengthens the sovereignty of Germany, and of Europe more broadly, in critical raw materials. These are exactly the kinds of leaps we want to make possible.”
cylib’s first industrial site, in Wernberg-Köblitz in eastern Bavaria, has been taking in end-of-life EV batteries and processing them into black mass since September 2026. The plant is ramping up step by step and is designed to handle up to 10,000 metric tons a year. In Dormagen, North Rhine-Westphalia, the company is building its large-scale hydrometallurgical plant. The European Commission has selected the project as a Strategic Project under the Critical Raw Materials Act.
Dr. Gideon Schwich,
co-CEO and co-founder of cylib, says:

Ampace Highlights AIDC Battery Safety and Semi-Solid-State Technology for AI Data Centres
At Data Centre World Paris, Ampace showcased its PU200 UPS battery system, built with semi-solid-state cells. Recent large-scale fire testing of the PU100 provides evidence of the company’s approach to system safety.
PARIS, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — At Data Centre World Paris 2026, Ampace showcased how it designs batteries for a critical moment in an AI data centre: when the mains supply fails and the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) must immediately carry the load. Its PU200 battery system combines high-rate discharge capability with a compact cabinet for facilities where space for backup power is limited.
Ampace develops the cells, modules and complete battery systems used in its data centre portfolio. Its engineers work from the requirements of the installation back to the cell itself. The power a UPS must deliver guides cell design, the heat generated during discharge informs thermal management, and the space available in the facility shapes the cabinet. Safety and reliability are design priorities at each stage.
Battery safety, from cell design to large-scale fire testing
A UPS battery can spend long periods on standby before it is called on to deliver high power within seconds. Ampace designs its cells with low internal resistance to limit heat generation during high-rate discharge and support reliable power delivery until an alternative supply takes over.
To assess how a complete battery system behaves under fire conditions, Ampace subjected its PU100 UPS battery system to large-scale fire testing under the sixth edition of UL 9540A. The PU100 met the applicable test criteria. For data centre operators evaluating battery fire risk, the results provide evidence of how the tested system performed under those conditions.
Semi-solid-state cells for high-power backup
The PU200 brings Ampace’s semi-solid-state lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cell technology into a UPS battery cabinet. Its cells support the short, high-power discharge required during a supply interruption, while the compact cabinet gives operators more flexibility when allocating floor space in an existing facility or planning a new modular data centre. A detachable battery management system simplifies access for servicing.

content:
JA ESS launches in-house battery passport platform to support EU compliance
BEIJING, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — JA ESS has launched an in-house battery passport platform designed to support lifecycle information management and help businesses prepare for upcoming EU requirements. The platform is hosted in the company’s own cloud environment, giving its team direct responsibility for data policies, access permissions and future updates.
Under the EU Batteries Regulation, battery passports will be required from 18 February 2027 for light means of transport (LMT) batteries, electric vehicle batteries and industrial batteries with a capacity greater than 2 kWh placed on the market or put into service. Further requirements will follow.
A battery passport is a digital record linked to an individual physical battery. A QR code and a unique identifier based on the ISO/IEC 15459 series connect the record to the battery and provide access to information across its lifecycle. This can include product identity, material composition, carbon footprint, recycled content, performance and durability, state of health, supply chain due diligence and end-of-life treatment. Together, these data points support consistent information management from product identification through end of life.
For manufacturers, the challenge is not simply creating a QR code. Data must be traceable to its source, kept current and made accessible in line with regulatory and business requirements. Companies also need to manage access to sensitive information and account for rules on cross-border data transfers and trade secrets. This balance is especially relevant for businesses operating across multiple markets. When companies rely on a third-party platform, its functions, data-field access and interoperability may be shaped by the provider’s configuration and service model.
JA ESS developed the platform in-house and hosts it in its own cloud environment. The platform’s data policies, access permissions and future updates are managed by JA ESS’s in-house team. It supports EU requirements for data access, presentation and updates while giving JA ESS greater oversight of data management. The platform can also evolve as regulatory requirements develop and practical applications provide further experience.
JA ESS is the energy storage business unit under the master brand JA. As a key part of JA’s energy storage strategy, JA ESS serves diverse FTM and BTM applications with safe, efficient, intelligent and customized solutions for utility-scale, C&I and residential markets.

ADS-TEC Energy Secures Repeat Order from German Utility SWLB for Large-Scale Battery Storage Systems
Delivery of an ADS-TEC Energy BESS5000 battery storage system to German municipal utility Stadtwerke Ludwigsburg-Kornwestheim (SWLB). Following its successful commissioning, SWLB has ordered two additional systems with a combined capacity of 10 MWh
Stadtwerke Ludwigsburg-Kornwestheim (SWLB) places repeat order for two additional ADS-TEC Energy battery storage systems with a combined capacity of 10 megawatt-hours
The new systems will increase flexibility in the local power grid and support the development of a resilient, decentralized energy infrastructure
Battery storage technology developed and integrated in Germany
NÜRTINGEN, Germany & LUDWIGSBURG, Germany–(
BUSINESS WIRE
)–ADS-TEC Energy has secured a repeat order from German municipal utility Stadtwerke Ludwigsburg-Kornwestheim (SWLB) for two additional battery energy storage systems. The two BESS5000 systems have a combined capacity of 10 megawatt-hours and will be installed at the Reuteallee site in Ludwigsburg. Commissioning is scheduled for summer 2027.
Only about a year ago, SWLB placed an order with ADS-TEC Energy for a 5-megawatt-hour battery storage system, which is now operational at the utility’s wood-fired combined heat and power plant in Ludwigsburg. The new order builds on the successful collaboration between the two companies.
German Battery Storage Technology for Municipal Energy Infrastructure
SWLB is pursuing a decentralized energy storage strategy, deploying multiple battery storage systems across its service area. The systems are designed to facilitate the integration of renewable energy, reduce strain on the power grid and create additional opportunities to participate in energy markets.
ADS-TEC Energy develops its battery storage technology in Germany and integrates the key technical components into a precisely matched overall system.

We are pleased that SWLB has once again placed its trust in us and that we are continuing our successful collaboration.
”When building a decentralized energy storage infrastructure, it is essential that individual systems operate reliably and integrate seamlessly into existing systems. This is where we contribute our many years of experience in developing and integrating battery storage systems. The project shows that, in this area of critical infrastructure, local partnerships lead to effective solutions.”
Sebastian Hess,
Strategy and Corporate Development at Stadtwerke Ludwigsburg, adds:
The additional storage systems are a key component for a future-ready energy infrastructure and support the expansion of renewable energy in the region.
”By participating in the balancing market, we also aim to contribute to grid stability.”

title: Fox ESS Delivers a 6MW/14.21MWh Battery Energy Storage Project in Trutnov, Czech Republic - Batteries News
content:
Fox ESS Delivers a 6MW/14.21MWh Battery Energy Storage Project in Trutnov, Czech Republic
TRUTNOV, Czech Republic, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Fox ESS, a global leader in renewable energy solutions, is further strengthening its strategic partnership with NOBILITY s.r.o. through a new 6MW/14.21MWh battery energy storage project in Trutnov, Czech Republic.
Located in Náchodsk, 541 03 Trutnov 3-Poříčí, the project is owned by ZEMKON Stare Buky s.r.o. and developed by NOBILITY s.r.o., with Fox ESS providing an integrated battery energy storage solution designed to support electricity price arbitrage, optimize energy management and unlock greater value from energy assets.
Fox ESS was selected for its strong delivery capabilities and comprehensive on-site service support. These strengths provide the customer with greater confidence in project execution and long-term system support.
Flexible Energy Trading for Greater Economic Value
At the heart of the Trutnov project is electricity price arbitrage. By storing electricity during low-price periods and discharging it when prices rise, Fox ESS’s battery energy storage system enables the customer to take advantage of market price fluctuations, optimize electricity trading strategies and unlock greater economic value from stored energy. This approach also enhances the flexibility and overall utilization of energy assets.
Integrated System Configuration for Efficient Deployment
The project features a total rated power output of 6MW and an energy storage capacity of 14.21MWh, connected to the grid at 35kV. The system comprises two 5,015kWh battery containers and one 4,180kWh battery container, paired with two power conversion system (PCS) skids rated at 4,000kVA and 2,000kVA, respectively.
Reliable Delivery and Localized Service Support
The equipment was delivered on August 11, 2026, and construction commenced on October 11, 2026. Grid connection and commissioning are preliminarily scheduled for December 30, 2026. With timely delivery and strong on-site service support, Fox ESS is committed to ensuring smooth project implementation and reliable system operation.
The Trutnov project marks another step in Fox ESS’s expansion in the Czech energy storage market. By combining integrated energy storage technology with flexible energy management capabilities and dependable service support, Fox ESS continues to empower customers to optimize energy consumption, unlock the economic potential of energy storage and contribute to a smarter, more sustainable energy future.

title: Elon Musk freezes at awkward Tesla Argentina launch: 'I don't know what to say'
content:
Fred Lambert
| Nov 21 2026 - 7:11 am PT
Tesla officially launched in Argentina on Friday with President Javier Milei on stage in Buenos Aires, and Elon Musk joined by video from his plane to welcome the brand’s newest market. It didn’t go well.
Musk got through one line about Tesla before stalling out: “Sorry, I don’t really know what I want to say.” The call ended about two minutes in, without any real pitch for the Model 3 or Model Y that Tesla had just put on sale.
Two minutes of “I don’t know what to say”
The launch took place at Arenas Studio in Buenos Aires’ La Boca neighborhood. Milei spoke for less than eight minutes, then the host asked the room to welcome “our next guest,” and Musk popped up on the giant screen from what looked like an airplane cabin. Milei burst out laughing and bounced on his feet.
Musk started fine: “Hello, Argentina. Well, here we are. It’s a joy to share Tesla with all of you and to establish ourselves there.”
JAJAJAJ QUE ES ESTO, Milei lo llamó de sorpresa a Elon Musk para que diga algo sobre el local de Tesla inaugurado y es lo mas INCÓMODO que vas a ver en tu vida, se quería ir a la mierda y COLGÓ, durísimo, ni Elon Musk lo soporta al gordo pelotudo
Then he started glancing off to each side. “Actually, I don’t really know what to say, other than thank you for this welcome to Tesla in Argentina,” he said. He briefly mentioned a charging network with state-owned oil company YPF, thanked the audience again, and then: “Sorry, I don’t really know what I want to say.”
And that was it. The feed cut before he even said goodbye.
Milei tried to save it. Back on stage, he told the crowd that “those who do a lot, talk little,” and called Musk “the Leonardo da Vinci of the 21st century.”
The clip is now spreading fast in Argentina, with
one post of the video
racking up over 1.1 million views overnight.
What Tesla is selling in Argentina
Tesla opened online orders on Friday for five versions of the Model 3 and Model Y, all imported from Gigafactory Shanghai. Here are the list prices, VAT included:
Model 3 RWD: $40,990
Model Y Premium RWD: $43,990
Model 3 Premium Long Range: $46,490
Model Y Premium Long Range: $49,990
Model 3 Performance: $53,990
Tesla adds about $600 in reservation, destination, and documentation fees on top of that, and first deliveries aren’t expected until March or April 2027. There are no dealers. Sales happen online, with showroom space at the Unicenter and Alcorta Shopping malls in Buenos Aires.
Argentina is Tesla’s fourth direct-sales market in South America after Chile, Colombia, and
Uruguay, which launched in July
. Tesla is late to the party, though. BYD already leads Argentina’s EV market after Milei’s government cut import taxes on electric vehicles.
Electrek’s Take
That was awkward. Like, really awkward.
I am sure Musk has a lot on his mind right now, but selling Tesla vehicles clearly isn’t one of them, because he couldn’t come up with anything to say about it.
Launching a new market has one job: get people excited to buy the cars. Musk had a sitting president cheering for him on stage, a room full of fans, and every camera in Buenos Aires pointed at him. He couldn’t come up with a single reason to buy a Model Y.
This isn’t stage fright. Musk has been telling investors for two years that Tesla’s future is robotaxis and Optimus robots, not selling cars. Meanwhile, Tesla’s deliveries fell 8.6% to 1.636 million in 2025, its second annual decline in a row. The guy who is behind the brand doesn’t care about selling these cars anymore, and this clip shows it better than anything I’ve seen.

title: CATL, BYD, ACWA among co-initiators of storage alliance unveiled at COP31 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
An international energy storage cooperation initiative backed by 27 companies and institutions has been formally launched at the UN climate conference in Turkey.
Vincent Shaw
21 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
The Global Energy Storage Alliance founded at COP31
The Global Energy Storage Alliance, known as GESA, was launched on Nov. 13 at the China Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, bringing together 27 co-initiating organizations spanning battery manufacturers, power utilities, state-owned enterprises, and research institutions from China and several other countries.
The three founding organizations are the China Energy Storage Alliance, the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute, and China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage Co. The co-initiator list includes battery and system manufacturers such as CATL, BYD Energy Storage, EVE Energy, Hithium, and Sungrow, alongside state-owned energy groups including CGN Energy International and POWERCHINA International. Saudi Arabian utility developer ACWA Power is among the international co-initiators. Seven organizations — including the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, the International Hydropower Association, Energy Storage Europe, and the World Resources Institute are listed as interested in exploring participation in GESA.
The launch event was attended by Liu Zhenmin, China’s Special Envoy for Climate Change; Francesco La Camera, Director-General of the International Renewable Energy Agency; Armida Salsiah Alisjahbana, UN Under-Secretary-General and Executive Secretary of ESCAP; and Xiong Minfeng, Deputy Director-General of the International Cooperation Department at China’s National Energy Administration.
GESA’s founding declaration outlines six areas of focus: facilitating international dialogue, building a global storage project and standards database, supporting research and technology deployment, improving market mechanisms, strengthening supply chains and trade, and mobilizing investment for projects in developing economies. The initiative describes itself as open, technology-neutral, and market-oriented, and states it will respect different national regulatory models.
Speaking at the launch, Sun Liqun, Deputy General Manager of China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage, identified three structural barriers the initiative aims to address: inadequate market mechanisms for valuing both short- and long-duration storage, fragmented technical standards and regulatory frameworks across countries, and financing and development barriers in emerging economies. These are widely recognized constraints on storage deployment. However, how the degree to which a voluntary industry alliance can move them will depend on the engagement it obtains beyond the launch.
Beyond industry coordination, the alliance carries weight in the UN-led climate process. Storage underpins the global push to triple renewable capacity by 2030, and GESA’s focus on technical assistance, capacity building and de-risked financing for developing economies speaks directly to the Paris Agreement’s call for an equitable transition. By channeling South-South cooperation toward emerging markets in Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Latin America, where financing costs remain the biggest obstacle to deployment, the initiative could help narrow the energy access gap between developed and developing countries.
For China, it marks a step from exporting storage products toward shaping global standards, extending its climate diplomacy from setting targets to building a system that deliver them.

title: Celebrating men, challenging stereotypes, building a stronger energy future together - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
On International Men’s Day, and as Movember raises awareness of men’s health and wellbeing, Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) and Solar+ Leaders celebrate the men across the solar and wider energy transition industries who are helping build a more inclusive future. Carmen Madrid, Founder of both initiatives, draws on perspectives shared throughout the network’s pv magazine series to reflect on why gender equality is not about women versus men, but about creating workplaces where everyone can thrive, lead authentically and contribute their full potential to the energy transition.
Women in Solar+ Europe
21 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Someone once asked me why I had decided to create a women’s network in the solar industry. My answer was simple: “Because our industry is full of good men who already want to change the world, and I couldn’t think of better ground on which to build a network that could help us change it together.”
On International Men’s Day, Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) wants to celebrate the men across our solar, energy storage and wider energy transition industries. The men who recognise talent beyond gender, challenge stereotypes, encourage others to grow and understand that creating a more inclusive industry is a shared responsibility. Many do so without recognition, through everyday decisions that shape careers, workplaces and opportunities for others.
Our industry has something extraordinary in common: a purpose that goes far beyond individual careers or commercial success. We are working towards a more sustainable, secure and resilient energy future. And that shared ambition gives us powerful common ground to rethink not only how we produce energy, but how we work together.
Beyond stereotypes: Equality benefits everyone
Gender equality is sometimes presented as a competition between women and men, as though creating opportunities for one group necessarily means taking something away from another. Yet the experiences shared throughout our Women in Solar+ Europe series suggest a different reality. Inclusion is about removing limitations, not creating new ones, and allowing people to contribute according to their abilities rather than expectations attached to their gender.
Antonio Arruebo, Senior Market Analyst at SolarPower Europe, captured this perspective in our previous reflections on gender equality: “Gender equality liberates everyone.” His message challenges us to recognise that stereotypes restrict men too, particularly when leadership is associated with authority, certainty or emotional restraint. Creating more inclusive workplaces also creates space for men to lead differently, express vulnerability and develop their own potential.
This is an important conversation for an industry that needs increasingly diverse capabilities. Technical expertise remains essential, but so do empathy, collaboration, adaptability and the ability to bring people together around complex challenges. None of these qualities belongs exclusively to one gender.
The courage to question ourselves
Progress also requires the courage to acknowledge that none of us is free from bias. We all develop assumptions through our upbringing, education and professional experiences. What matters is whether we are willing to recognise them and reconsider how they influence our decisions.
Emiliano Bellini, News Director at
pv magazine
, explored this in his contribution to our series, encouraging open conversations and greater tolerance for mistakes when addressing unconscious bias. His message was clear: “We must free our thinking and allow room for mistakes.”
This is particularly relevant when engaging more men in conversations about inclusion. Fear of saying the wrong thing should not prevent participation. We need environments where people can ask questions, disagree respectfully, learn from different perspectives and evolve together. Inclusion cannot flourish if conversations become another space where people feel judged rather than encouraged to grow.
Of course, positive intentions must translate into action. The real test of inclusive leadership comes through everyday decisions about recruitment, recognition, promotion and professional development.
Josef Kastner, CEO of Nexun, addressed this responsibility in his contribution to the series, highlighting how conscious and unconscious bias influences career opportunities. His position was unequivocal: “Everyone deserves the same rights and opportunities.” Kastner also shared how he challenged inappropriate behaviour towards a female manager, demonstrating that allyship is not simply about supporting equality in principle. It means being prepared to act when fairness is compromised, even when those conversations are uncomfortable.
Frank Niendorf, Vice President Europe at JinkoSolar, offered a complementary perspective on the evolution of leadership and the importance of creating inclusive working environments. He highlighted that effective leadership goes beyond traditional notions of authority and assertiveness. It is about fostering open dialogue, listening actively and encouraging diverse perspectives, ensuring that everyone feels empowered to contribute. His perspective reinforces how challenging conventional leadership stereotypes can help create stronger, more collaborative teams.
This conversation feels particularly relevant during Movember, a global movement raising awareness of men’s mental and physical health, including mental health and suicide prevention, prostate cancer and testicular cancer. In industries like ours, where demanding targets, constant change and high levels of responsibility are part of everyday life, we should also question the expectations placed on men to always appear strong, confident and in control. Creating psychologically safe workplaces means ensuring that men, too, feel comfortable expressing vulnerability, asking for support and speaking openly about their wellbeing. An inclusive culture should not only help women overcome the barriers they face; it should also help men overcome the expectations that hold them back.
These reflections matter because organisational cultures are shaped by what leaders encourage, tolerate and challenge. The men who question their own assumptions, sponsor emerging talent, share recognition and create opportunities for others contribute directly to building stronger, more capable teams.
Leadership is ultimately about people
The energy transition is often discussed through gigawatts, investment, infrastructure and technological innovation. Yet behind every project are people whose ability to collaborate determines whether those ambitions become reality.
Kim Keats, Partner at Ekon Strategy Consulting, offered a timely reminder in his contribution to our series: “Our industry is ultimately about people, not just technology, models or spreadsheets.”
His reflections highlighted the importance of trust, meaningful dialogue and listening to perspectives that might otherwise be overlooked. Similarly, Jesús Alijarde, General Director of Ibersyd/Cerfo, emphasised the importance of creating environments where employees feel safe enough to challenge decisions openly. “Showing your team that you do not know everything and that you also make mistakes allows the organisation to grow much faster together,” he explained in our
pv magazine
Both perspectives point towards a leadership model that values people as individuals rather than simply resources. They also challenge the traditional expectation that leaders, particularly men, must always project certainty and have all the answers. This becomes increasingly important as our industries navigate rapid technological change, growing complexity and the integration of artificial intelligence into everyday work.
A shared responsibility for the future
At Women in Solar+ Europe, we have always believed that building a more inclusive industry requires women and men working together. We need men who are willing to listen, challenge inherited assumptions and recognise that supporting others does not diminish their own achievements. Equally, we need to create spaces where men can participate authentically, without being reduced to stereotypes or expected to have every answer.
This belief is so central to our mission that it led us to create Solar+ Leaders, our leadership development ecosystem open to everyone across the solar and wider energy transition industries, regardless of gender. Through mentoring, leadership development, shared learning and meaningful connections, we are building a community where people can grow together, challenge their assumptions and develop the human capabilities our industries need to navigate an increasingly complex future.
Because Solar+ Leaders is not a place where we talk about inclusive leadership. It is where we nurture it and put it into practice. And where we recognise that the energy transition is not only a technological challenge; it is a leadership challenge.
On this International Men’s Day, our message is one of appreciation to the many men who contribute to our industry with integrity, generosity and a genuine desire to make a difference. Those who mentor, encourage, collaborate, open doors and help others discover what they are capable of achieving.
Leadership has no gender; it has values. And perhaps the greatest opportunity before us is to build an industry where those values allow everyone to thrive.
Because the energy transition is not a competition between women and men. It is a collective mission that needs the very best of all of us.

title: Unigrid looks to fill gaps in lithium-ion storage with effective sodium-ion alternatives - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
CEO Darren Tan says sodium-ion batteries can compete on safety, performance and price in key market segments.
Michael Puttré
21 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Energy Storage
San Diego-based Unigrid is hoping to make sodium-ion a household name. The company’s development team grew out of research centered on the University of California, San Diego, with the goal of providing battery storage technology to serve the markets where lithium-ion is not as suitable.
Unigrid CEO Darren Tan
told pv magazine USA
that while there are many categories in which lithium ion does well, sodium-ion battery chemistries have advantages in important market segments.
“You’ve got better safety,” Tan said, indicating sodium-ion chemistries are not flammable. “You’ve got extremely long cycle and calendar life. Sodium just doesn’t die. Also, sodium chemistries have great thermal tolerance; they don’t care how hot it is in summer or how cold it is winter. The biggest disadvantage of the batteries is that they are heavier and take up a little more space.”
The company says its 48V Na+ Casa series batteries, which are positioned for commercial and residential storage, have a discharge temperature range of about -100°F to +140°F and will charge down to about -68°F. They are UN38.3 certified and tested to UL 9540A standards at the cell level. The fire resistance of sodium-ion chemistries makes the suitable for deployment indoors, such as in hospitals or multi-unit housing.
At the same time, residential and commercial storage remains dominated by lithium-ion battery makers that are well ensconced with recognized brands with ever-increasing track records.
While there are examples of alternate chemistries and technologies, such as flow batteries, making inroads in the market, these suppliers face an uphill climb.
It is tempting, Tan says, to lump battery storage into a single category, but in reality, it is many, many vertical market segments. Lithium-ion chemistries, he concedes, have come to dominate the midrange endurance needs, from two to about six hours. Moreover, they are favored in many applications, from portable devices, to vehicles to grid-connected BESS. One aspect of this dominance is that suppliers and developers using them have ready access to financing.
Lithium-ion solutions are bankable, even standard, which industry analysts have pointed out may deter the development and deployment of more appropriate technologies in key markets. At the same time, Tan says sodium-ion is starting to get its strides in certain sectors, for example the short duration space.
For many years, there was no real demand to fill the gap between very short-duration – minutes or even seconds – applications provided by supercapacitors and the mid-range provided by batteries. However, Tan says, the advent of AI began producing strains on the grid, with demand moving from traditional arbitrage into things like ancillary services.
“You’ve got to service things like demand response,” Tan said. “You’ve got to provide capacity for uninterruptible loads; you’ve got to provide short demand charges based on load shifting. And lithium-ion is not great for that kind of high-power quick response. It also doesn’t like multiple cycles. Short-duration storage in data centers may need to cycle 10, 20 times a day, especially if you’re looking at an AI model training context.”
According to Tan, the prevailing solution has been to use lithium-titanate oxide (LTO) batteries, which have better cycling performance, charge and discharge rates, and operational temperature ranges than lithium-ion. LTO is also much more expensive, coming in at 20 times the cost of lithium-ion.
“Sodium-ion checks all the boxes,” Tan said. “High power, very long cycle life, wide temperature ranges so you don’t have to cool it, and it’s also very safe. And we can compete on price.”
Overall, Tan said the most significant challenges Unigrid faces with its sodium-ion batteries are achieving the third-party testing benchmarks and winning necessary regulatory certification for widespread deployment in the U.S. Lithium-ion BESS suppliers have already cleared many of these hurdles. Tan says Unigrid is looking to its installations in Europe and other parts of the world to support its plans for succeeding in the U.S. market. He is hopeful that increasing demand and the rising price of diesel and other fuels will prompt developers – and financiers – to take a good look at sodium-ion batteries.
A recent study by Wood Mackenzie identifies sodium-ion batteries as the most promising emerging alternative to lithium-based technologies for stationary energy storage. Manufacturers are expected to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate batteries by late 2026, while parity at the module and system levels is not expected until after 2030.

content:
Markets & Policy
The new framework introduces energy and water efficiency standards, renewable electricity procurement obligations, and grid flexibility requirements for data centers. A €17.14 billion transmission network plan will support 47.4 GW of new electricity demand through 2030.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
21 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
The Spanish government approved a royal decree on Nov. 20 establishing energy sustainability, environmental, resilience and digital sovereignty requirements for data centers. The Council of Ministers also approved the country’s electricity transmission network development plan through 2030, which was presented last week.
Third Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Ecological Transition Sara Aagesen announced the measures following the cabinet meeting.
The regulation comes amid rapid growth in electricity demand from data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure. According to Aagesen, data center projects have secured grid access permits for 15 GW of capacity, including 6 GW on the transmission network and 9 GW on distribution networks. This represents nearly 40% of Spain’s peak electricity demand, while a further 20 GW of capacity is awaiting grid access.
These figures significantly exceed the projections in Spain’s 2024 Artificial Intelligence Strategy, which anticipated less than 4 GW of data center electricity demand by 2030.
The government had already raised concerns about the potential impact of large-scale data center development on electricity demand, grid capacity and renewable energy deployment. In August, it
proposed requiring data centers to source at least 80% of their electricity from additional renewable generation
Renewable energy and efficiency requirements
The approved decree introduces several changes to the initial proposal published in August, including a higher capacity threshold for the main requirements.
The revised framework targets data centers with grid access capacity of at least 10 MW, up from the 1 MW threshold initially proposed. It establishes requirements covering renewable electricity procurement, energy and water efficiency, grid flexibility, resilience and digital sovereignty.
Data centers must demonstrate that at least 80% of their annual electricity consumption is covered by on-site renewable generation or long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) with new renewable energy facilities.
The decree also introduces hourly matching requirements between electricity consumption and renewable generation, with a phased implementation period extending to 2032. Eligible facilities can follow a transitional compliance pathway, subject to conditions including participation in demand reduction mechanisms.
The regulation requires qualifying facilities to meet class A standards under the European classification systems for power usage effectiveness (PUE) and water usage effectiveness (WUE). Energy efficiency requirements will also take account of regional climatic conditions.
For water consumption, the government has established a target of 0.1 liters per kWh to achieve the highest efficiency classification.
The decree also links grid access and connection rights to compliance with the new requirements. Data centers may be required to reduce electricity demand or disconnect loads during periods of grid congestion or system stress.
Aagesen described Spain as a pioneer in regulating the energy and environmental impact of data centers.
The government estimates that, without the regulation, the expansion of data centers could add €5 billion annually to electricity costs and increase electricity bills for industrial consumers by 25%.
The measures come as Spain faces growing pressure to accommodate new electricity demand while managing grid constraints. The country has also been examining
grid congestion and renewable energy curtailment risks
as solar and other renewable energy capacity expands.
Grid plan through 2030
Alongside the data center decree, the Council of Ministers approved an updated electricity transmission network development plan through 2030, with planned investment of €17.14 billion ($18.82 billion).
The plan allocates grid capacity to accommodate 47.4 GW of new electricity demand, including 14.9 GW for industry, 12.4 GW for renewable hydrogen, 9.3 GW for data centers and 6 GW for residential and urban development.
It also includes approximately 6,707 km of new transmission lines, upgrades to increase capacity across 8,164 km of existing lines, and 193 substations.
The investment represents a substantial increase over earlier proposals. In September, Spain
raised planned grid investment above €17 billion and announced a capacity market
to support generation, energy storage and demand-side flexibility.
The expansion of transmission infrastructure is intended to support the electrification of industry, renewable hydrogen production and other emerging sources of electricity demand, while facilitating the integration of additional renewable energy capacity.
Spain’s growing electricity demand has become an increasingly important factor in renewable energy development. According to figures published by Spanish solar association UNEF, the country had
71.5 GW of demand connection capacity either granted or included in grid planning through 2030
, with a further 24 GW of pending requests.
The approval of the data center decree and transmission network plan establishes a new regulatory and infrastructure framework for accommodating electricity demand from AI infrastructure and other energy-intensive activities, while linking new data center development to renewable generation and grid flexibility requirements.

title: The U.S. solar manufacturing landscape in 2026 - pv magazine Global
content: There is a group of about 40 companies that are actively producing silicon PV components in the United States, from polysilicon to modules, each with a different growth model out to 2030. While the landscape remains somewhat fragmented, there are signs that a consolidated production-led approach could emerge in the coming years, particularly if the sector can unite on a technology roadmap and the need for a domestic materials-based supply chain. The starting point to understand the U.S. solar PV manufacturing landscape is the capital expenditure (capex) committed by the different companies active in the sector. Capex forms the basis of the investments into new factories and production equipment, ultimately creating the basis of future production activity. The capex trends from 2020 to 2026 reveal a clustering into specific states or regions that have been prioritized by domestic solar manufacturers. This is shown in the chart below, with the key spending regions for 2026 segmented to assess the future growth potential in production volumes from 2027 onwards. Texas is the leading state for PV capex in 2026, with key contributions from Canadian Solar’s module expansion in Mesquite, near Dallas, the build-out of the new manufacturing base by SpaceX in Bastrop, east of Austin, SEG Solar’s new module base at Tomball, northwest of Houston, and T1 Energy’s new cell factory outside of Austin. Collectively, these four companies make up about 90% of the total PV capex in Texas during 2026, with nine other entities contributing to the residual Texas capex total. The next major spending region in 2026 is the Carolinas. This is driven by Boviet Solar’s spending on its cell factory in Greenville, North Carolina, First Solar’s new module assembly factory in Gaffney, South Carolina, and ES Foundry’s cell expansion in Greenwood, South Carolina. An additional six companies have meaningful capex allocations in the Carolinas during 2026, with the most significant coming from early spending from Suniva for its new cell factory in Laurens, South Carolina. The next region of spending activity segmented in the chart comes from other companies allocating capex to sites across other Southeastern states. This zone includes First Solar’s existing factories in Trinity, Alabama, and New Iberia in Louisiana that were built out mainly during 2023 to 2025. Qcells’ ingot-to-module Cartersville base northwest of Atlanta, Georgia, also falls into this segmented territory, with the spending by Qcells also concentrated in the period from 2023 to 2025. Another six companies contribute to the 2026 capex levels, but at much lower levels of spending. The final region of capex significance spans the Midwest states of Indiana, Michigan, and Ohio. Spending here is led by Canadian Solar’s new cell factory in Jeffersonville, Indiana, alongside Corning’s ongoing capital deployment across the company’s co-located polysilicon and ingot/wafer manufacturing bases in Saginaw County, northwest of Detroit, Michigan. Other contributions in 2026 come from First Solar’s spending at its three-plant manufacturing cluster south of Toledo, Ohio, adjacent to Perrysburg Township and Lake Township. Module clusters While the long-term goal of capex into U.S. solar manufacturing is to develop all stages in the value-chain, the major investments since the introduction of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022 have been into module assembly facilities. Therefore, a detailed regional analysis of production activity in the United States is today confined to module. This is likely to change in the coming years, but will depend ultimately on the capex allocated to silicon cells and ingots/wafers during 2027 and 2028. This is shown on the chart below. During the past couple of years, module production volumes in the United States have been increasingly dominated by Texas, from Canadian Solar in Mesquite, T1 Energy’s Wilmer plant south of Dallas, SEG Solar’s two module bases outside Houston, Imperial Star’s Tomball factory north of Houston, Waaree Energies in Brookshire west of Houston, TOYO in Humble, northeast of Houston, and Elin Elektrik’s Sirius Solar operations in Brookshire. About 95% of solar module production in Texas during 2026 is forecast to come from factories located in a 50-mile radius within the Greater Houston region and a 25-mile radius within the Greater Dallas region, representing more than one-quarter of all module production in the United States. The other major state for module production is Ohio. In contrast to the activity in Texas across a range of different companies, module production in Ohio is almost exclusively coming from First Solar’s thin-film lines and Illuminate’s silicon module assembly base. The third major module production area in 2026 comes from a specific group of states in the Southeast – South Carolina, North Carolina, Georgia and Alabama. Volumes are dominated by Qcells in Dalton and Cartersville, Georgia, First Solar in Alabama, and Inox Clean Energy’s at the former Boviet Solar site in North Carolina. A further seven companies across South Carolina, Georgia and Alabama are also producing modules in 2026. Industry leaders While nameplate capacity announcements and aspirations have been covered extensively in the United States since the introduction of the Inflation Reduction Act, manufacturing activity is best understood through analyzing the capex and production output from company-specific manufacturing plants – the basis of a new methodology developed by Terawatt PV Research to benchmark and rate U.S. solar manufacturers. The methodology behind company-specific rankings (overall manufacturing strength scores) and ratings (from AAA-rated to C-rated) involves weighted analysis of production volumes and manufacturing capex and a minimum threshold, followed by normalization and z-score analysis. The ratings pyramid (left) for the third quarter of 2026 highlights the importance of companies in the United States that are active across more than one stage of the value-chain. First Solar is the only company to feature in the top AAA-rated band, with its thin-film manufacturing process flow equal to the whole silicon-based value-chain. Corning is AA-rated, mainly through its polysilicon, ingot, wafer and module operations in Michigan and Arizona. Canadian Solar is the other AA-rated company with meaningful production and capex contributions from its module base in Texas and cell plant in Indiana. Across the lower B- and C-rating bands, companies are generally pure-play module producers, such as SEG Solar, Illuminate and Waaree Energies, or focused on cell manufacturing, such as Suniva and ES Foundry. As more silicon-based companies backward integrate from module to cell production, a greater number will feature in the A to AAA-rated bands from 2027 onwards. The pyramid will also see changes next year as legacy site contributions in 2026 from JinkoSolar and Boviet Solar transition to new owners. In particular, Inox Clean Energy is expected to see a strong upward tick once Boviet’s new cell factory is sold to Inox in 2027. Expectations for 2027 With module-based capex having dominated the domestic solar investment landscape since 2023, the next stage of onshoring the silicon-based ecosystem will come from new capital released to increase domestic cell production volumes, in addition to building key materials supply options for module production (including encapsulant films, backsheets, glass and frames). Ultimately, the long-term success of a domestic solar ecosystem in the United States will not simply come from a group of leading companies committing capex and running factories at high production volumes, but by the operations being profitable with a stable policy outlook. If this can be achieved, there is every chance that a U.S. solar manufacturing industry could become a reality. title: Battery patents: Solid-state filings surpass lithium-ion to hit record high - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Global solid-state battery patent filings hit a record 2,230 in 2024, up 16%, with South Korea overtaking Japan, driven by Samsung SDI’s rapid growth. Meanwhile, lithium-ion patent filings fell nearly 15% to 2,092, while sodium-ion filings dropped 29%, signaling a shift in battery innovation toward solid-state technologies.
Tristan Rayner
21 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Global patent filings for
solid-state batteries
reached a record 2,230 in 2024, up 16% from 2023. That’s according to the sixth annual Inside Green Innovation: Progress Report by intellectual property firm Appleyard Lees, which tracks patent filings across domains including food, such as cultivated meat, recycling, and fusion energy.
In contrast, lithium-ion battery patents across chemistries and applications fell nearly 15% to 2,092, with the data clerly showing consecutive years of declines. The report tracks complete public patent data through December 31, 2024, given delays across regions in visibility of applications.
Solid state
South Korea overtook Japan to lead global solid-state filings in 2024, posting 873 applications compared to Japan’s 605. Japan had held the top spot every year through 2023, but South Korea’s nearly 50% year-on-year surge, driven largely by
Samsung SDI
, shifted the balance. Samsung SDI nearly doubled its solid-state filings from 165 to 325, more than twice Toyota’s combined total of 144.
China ranked third in solid-state priority filings with 217, more than doubling its output since 2022, while Europe reached a record 177 filings. South Korea also maintained the lead in conventional lithium-ion filings, which nearly doubled from 441 in 2020 to 833 in 2024.
Chris Mason, Partner at Appleyard Lees, said solid-state electrolytes showed the strongest growth in the data, while lithium-ion technologies “appear to be consolidating, with filing numbers decreasing for a second consecutive year.”
In part, this reflections the maturing and commercialized supply chain around LFP cells for stationary energy storage. Patent volume is generally a lagging indicator of R&D spend.
Meanwhile,
sodium-ion
patent activity cooled after a record 2023, dropping 29% from 555 filings to 392, though still outpacing any year prior to 2022.
European organizations
filed a record 76 sodium-ion patents in 2024, taking second place behind China.
Appleyard Lees said “flow battery filings remain on a plateau” that began in 2016, even as grid-scale storage is deployed at record rates.
Fusion energy
Though not strictly related to energy storage, the annual coverage of fusion energy always reveals interesting trends in technology development. The report says, quote:
“Fusion is becoming a platform technology sector, as much as an energy sector, generating intellectual property with relevance far beyond future fusion power plants.
“Fusion research is inherently multidisciplinary. Delivering practical fusion energy requires breakthroughs across plasma physics, superconducting materials, advanced manufacturing, control systems, isotope handling, cryogenics and numerous other technical fields. Many of these technologies have applications in markets that are already established and considerably closer to commercial deployment than fusion power itself.”
“As a result, the fusion innovation landscape represents a rich source of intellectual property, licensing opportunities and potential spin-outs with relevance across sectors including semiconductors, healthcare, aerospace, energy infrastructure and advanced manufacturing.”
