title: Tariffs, taxes and a BESS price rise - pv magazine Global
content: US tariffs on battery energy storage system (BESS) imports rank among the steepest worldwide. Section 301 forced-labor duties have pushed effective tariffs on lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China to 40.9%, stacking on top of Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper. Battery cells are spared from Section 232, but auxiliary components are not. These include power control systems (PCS), connectors, and battery container enclosures. Combined tariffs add over $35/kWh to Chinese LFP BESS imports into the United States. Prices will rise to $195/kWh in 2027, nearly matching 2024 levels. In comparison, Europe’s much lower tariffs and labor costs keep prices down at around $140/kWh to $160/kWh. China’s domestic tax changes are adding further upward price pressure. The reapplication of the consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries and systems – rising from 2% to 4% in September 2027 – is pushing some producers to pass costs on to clients, compounded by a rise in China’s VAT rate on exports to 13% in 2027. Together, these tax changes alone are expected to add $4/kWh to the price of imported BESS for US buyers. BESS produced in the United States will also suffer a premium from recent policy changes. Restrictions on foreign-produced components as a result of the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) ban on new inverter models and Executive Order 14421 on Bulk Power Systems will drive US developers to source from compliant ­suppliers. US developers will have to pay more as supply from non-foreign entity of concern (FEOC) scales. These factors will keep US domestically produced LFP BESS prices elevated in 2027, with our domestic price forecast expected to exceed $205/kWh. Upstream materials Batteries and energy storage systems are as sensitive to upstream supply disruptions as solar PV has shown to be, due to their highly interconnected value chains. Battery-grade lithium chemical prices have surged across 2026, marking the sharpest rise since the peak in 2022. This is being driven by booming Chinese cathode output – up 67% year on year between January and July – which has collided with a lithium supply deficit deepened by an export ban in Zimbabwe and permitting delays at major mining sites in China. The latter includes the Jianxiawo lithium mine in China’s Jiangxi province, which has been closed since its previous mining license expired in August 2025. Lithium chemical prices will likely remain elevated into 2027 as supply lags the rally, before easing again as a surplus emerges – fed by restarted primary production, recycling output growth, and rising demand substitution from sodium-ion batteries. Lithium isn’t the only material under pressure. In August, major Chinese cathode producers raised prices by 5%, citing sulfur cost increases triggered by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Sulfur is essential for two key LFP ingredients: iron sulfate and technical monoammonium phosphate. Aluminum is facing similar strain, as reduced output from key Middle Eastern smelters have driven global stocks to a near 20-year low. Copper adds further weight, as reduced output from Chile meets surging demand from grid investment and downstream battery products like electric vehicles and BESS. The result is a system-wide cost effect that resonates across the entire value chain. These rising material costs alone are expected to lift global BESS prices by over $5/kWh in 2027 versus 2026. However, this trend will be short-lived. Higher prices should incentivize new supply across each material value chain, easing costs in the medium-term. Even so, the current squeeze underscores how cyclical supply-demand imbalances can ripple through to downstream pricing. Cutting-edge manufacturers still have a key lever in performance improvements. Higher-capacity, longer-life containers raise the kilowatt-hour denominator in $/kWh pricing, offsetting rising costs. Combined with component savings from system-level energy density gains, we expect BESS prices to fall beyond 2028 and into the 2030s. Import costs US policy has incentivized the build-out of LFP cathode active material (CAM) factories outside of China in an effort to remove bottlenecks in battery supply chains. Access to advanced manufacturing tax credits has been restricted to cellmakers with access to cathode active materials (CAM) supply outside of China, which has been effective in supporting scale-up of LFP CAM production in new regions. Production capacity outside of China will increase more than fivefold between 2026 and 2030. However, the tax credits come with strings attached. Sourcing from ex-China facilities is not enough to ensure eligibility. Operators with greater than 25% ownership from a single Chinese company are potentially deemed as prohibited foreign entities (PFEs), meaning customers could lose out on eligibility to the Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit (AMPC). This creates uncertainty over the eligibility status for 550 kt of LFP capacity operated outside China in 2030. Instead, likely eligible supply comes largely from two South Korean firms, L&F and Posco Future M. These companies have recently signed offtake with SK On and Samsung SDI, two of the three Korean cell makers that will supply most of America’s domestic BESS cells. The third, LG Energy Solution, uses a different strategy. LG has so far bought LFP CAM from LBM in Indonesia, despite LBM’s ownership including an effective 43.8% stake held by China’s Lopal. Despite this, LG Energy Solution has received tax credits because of safe harbor rules granted to agreements made before June 2025. But this only applies to material sold before the end of 2026. LG may therefore have to alter its sourcing strategy or influence change in LBM’s ownership to receive tax credits in 2027. Uncertainty when sourcing from Chinese overseas subsidiaries will create opportunities for new investment into localized supply chains. title: Chery’s V25 launches in China with 15-minute charging from 30% to 80%, uses 33.67-kwh battery
content: Chery’s iCar brand launched the V25 in China on November 19, adding a range-extended SUV to its boxy V-series lineup. The V25 is the third model in the series and comes in four trims, with limited-time prices ranging from about $17,900 to $22,400. The SUV combines a battery rated for about 130 miles of electric driving with a turbocharged gasoline engine that extends its claimed total range to more than 745 miles. The V25 first appeared in Chinese regulatory filings in July, four months before its launch. Up to 449 hp and a 15-minute charge The V25’s extended-range system uses a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine and delivers up to 449 hp and 372 lb-ft of torque. Chery puts the SUV’s acceleration from zero to roughly 62 mph in the five-second range. A 33.67-kWh lithium iron phosphate battery supplies power for electric driving. Chery says the pack can charge from 30 percent to 80 percent in 15 minutes. The electric-only range comes from the China Light-Duty Vehicle Test Cycle, a standardized laboratory test. On longer trips, the gasoline engine can generate electricity when the battery runs low. Drivers can plug the V25 in to replenish the battery between trips or refuel the SUV on the road. The combined range figure accounts for both energy sources. Boxy styling carries over from the V23 The V25 takes its upright shape from the V23, with steep front pillars, wide wheel arches, and a flat window line. It measures about 182.5 inches long with the rear storage box fitted, 75.6 inches wide and 73 inches tall. The wheelbase is about 111 inches. The SUV rides on 21-inch wheels with tires roughly 10.4 inches wide. It has 7.8 inches of ground clearance, a 30-degree approach angle and a 28-degree departure angle. Those angles indicate how steep a slope the SUV can approach or leave before its front or rear touches the ground. A 17-degree breakover angle describes the clearance available when crossing a crest. Chery offers five exterior colors. Buyers can choose from pearl white, black, silver, green, and matte gray. Removable trim makes room for accessories Chery designed the trim behind the rear side windows to come off so owners can fit accessories such as a ladder or a side storage box. The SUV also uses mechanical door handles that sit partly recessed into the body. At the rear, the design leaves room for decorative light boxes and features a “Lego-style” high-mounted brake light. The tailgate swings sideways and can hold its position anywhere along its travel. That lets owners open it partway when there is limited room for the gate to swing. A separate 0.8-cubic-foot compartment at the rear provides space for smaller items. The V25 also features Chery’s “Super Falcon 700+” driver-assistance system. It runs on a Horizon Robotics Journey 6P chip, which provides up to 560 trillion operations per second of computing power.

title: US nuclear rival’s 1,740-mile Kh-101 stealth cruise missile enters NATO-member Poland
content: ​A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Polish airspace before crashing roughly 31 miles (50 km) inside the country Friday, November 20. The crash was considered a serious violation of NATO territory since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. ​Polish authorities also reported two additional objects, believed to be another missile and a jet-powered drone, entering the country during Russia’s latest large-scale strike against Ukraine. ​The incident unfolded as Russia launched one of its largest overnight attacks of the war, firing more than 110 missiles alongside hundreds of drones against Ukrainian targets, according to Ukrainian and Polish officials. Poland scrambled F-16 fighters, activated Patriot air-defense batteries and coordinated with NATO surveillance assets after radar detected multiple objects approaching its eastern frontier. ​Raises concern for NATO For NATO, the concern extends well beyond a single missile. ​The Kh-101 is among Russia’s most advanced air-launched cruise missiles and was designed specifically to strike ground targets at long range, cruising at 435 mph (700 km/hr) with a reported maximum speed of 590 mph (900 km/hr). Carried primarily by Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers, the missile has an estimated range of up to 1,740 miles (2,800 km), allowing launch aircraft to remain deep inside Russian airspace while striking targets across Ukraine and much of Eastern Europe. ​It carries a conventional warhead weighing approximately 990 pounds (450 kg), though some modified variants reportedly feature dual-warhead configurations for increased destructive capacity. ​Unlike ballistic missiles that descend at hypersonic speeds, the Kh-101 flies at low altitude, hugging terrain and using onboard navigation systems to weave around natural obstacles. That flight profile significantly shortens radar detection windows, leaving defending forces with only minutes, or sometimes seconds, to classify and intercept an incoming threat. ​The missile combines inertial navigation, satellite guidance, and terrain-matching systems before relying on electro-optical guidance during its terminal phase. Military analysts said this layered navigation enables high accuracy against infrastructure, logistics hubs and command centers. ​Preferred combat weapon Since its combat debut in Syria, the Kh-101 has become one of Russia’s preferred long-range strike weapons during the war in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly used the missile in coordinated attacks alongside Kalibr sea-launched cruise missiles, Iskander ballistic missiles and large numbers of Shahed-type drones. The combination is intended to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses by forcing operators to engage multiple threats arriving from different directions and at varying speeds. ​The latest incident also underscores a growing risk for NATO countries bordering Ukraine. ​Although Poland has experienced previous incursions by Russian missiles and drones during major attacks on Ukraine, Friday’s event occurred amid multinational military exercises involving allied forces and renewed discussions over strengthening NATO’s eastern flank. ​Military experts noted that even if a cruise missile is not intended to strike NATO territory, its long range, terrain-following flight path and proximity to Ukraine’s western border create opportunities for navigation errors, battle damage or deliberate route changes that can carry it across international boundaries. ​Each incident forces allied commanders to decide within moments whether an unidentified object poses enough risk to justify interception, a decision with potentially far-reaching political and military consequences. ​

title: US Navy opens door to F-35C on Ford-class carriers after 34 flights
content: The US Navy has cleared the F-35C Lightning II to operate from all of its aircraft carrier classes after an 11-day trial aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy. Lockheed Martin announced the clearance on November 19 after testing showed the stealth fighter could use the Ford-class carrier’s electromagnetic catapult and new landing system. Two F-35Cs from Naval Air Station Patuxent River in Maryland completed 34 flights during the campaign. The aircraft logged 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings. The results open the way for the fighter to join air wings aboard Ford-class carriers, though the lead ship still needs upgrades before it can deploy with an F-35C squadron. How the Kennedy trials tested the F-35C The first arrested landing aboard John F. Kennedy took place on October 13. The at-sea evaluation followed shore tests that ran from January 2024 to May 2025, giving engineers a chance to check how the aircraft and the carrier’s equipment worked together on a ship at sea. The Kennedy uses the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System in place of the steam catapults found on Nimitz-class carriers. For landings, it uses Advanced Arresting Gear to slow an aircraft after its tailhook catches a cable stretched across the deck. Engineers monitored the loads on the fighter during launches and landings to help establish the conditions under which it can operate from the carrier. The team also reviewed what maintenance crews would need aboard the carrier to service the fighter during an extended deployment at sea. The software check was limited to an early look at stability aboard the new ship. Full operational validation of the Block 4 upgrade remains a separate step. Why USS Gerald R. Ford still needs upgrades The F-35C already serves aboard some Nimitz-class carriers, but USS Gerald R. Ford has yet to deploy with the fighter. The lead ship’s air wing has relied primarily on F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, alongside EA-18G Growlers that provide electronic warfare support. John F. Kennedy received changes during construction to accommodate the F-35C. Gerald R. Ford still needs modifications to its jet blast deflectors, which shield the flight deck from exhaust during launches, as well as secure spaces to support the aircraft. The Navy plans to make those changes ahead of future F-35C deployments. What the F-35C brings to Ford-class carriers The clearance covers the F-35C, the version built for catapult launches and arrested landings. It has larger wings with folding tips and reinforced landing gear for carrier operations. The Marine Corps primarily flies the F-35B, a short-takeoff and vertical-landing variant, from amphibious assault ships. Adding the F-35C to a Ford-class air wing would bring a stealth aircraft into a mix that already includes Super Hornets and Growlers. The aircraft combines information from its onboard sensors to give pilots a single view of their surroundings. It can also share information with other aircraft equipped to receive it. The tests will inform Navy guidance that specifies when the F-35C can safely launch from and land on Ford-class carriers . Before deploying an F-35C squadron, each ship will still need the facilities, maintenance support, and approved procedures to sustain the aircraft at sea.

title: China’s electric mining truck hauls 240 tons and charges to 90% in under an hour
content: A new electric mining truck from China can carry 240 tons of material and recharge from 20% to 90% in under an hour, according to its manufacturer. Inner Mongolia North Hauler Joint Stock Co. (NHL) developed the NTE240E for open-pit mines, where it can also draw electricity from overhead lines while hauling a load uphill. The rigid-frame truck is part of NHL’s push into battery-electric mining equipment. It combines a battery of up to 4.1 megawatt-hours (MWh) with two charging connections and regenerative braking. The manufacturer designed the truck to reduce charging downtime and lower the cost of hauling material compared with a diesel truck of similar capacity. Founded in 1988, NHL has supplied rigid-frame haul trucks to mines around the world, including models with diesel-electric drivetrains. Two plugs for 4.1-MWh battery The largest battery configuration holds 4,100 kilowatt-hours of energy. To replenish it, the NTE240E uses two plugs based on the Megawatt Charging System (MCS), an interface developed for high-power charging of heavy vehicles. NHL describes the dual-plug setup as a world first. The company says the truck can complete the 20 percent-to-90 percent charge at 77°F (25°C). On the largest battery, that window represents about 2.9 MWh of stored energy. The charging time could allow operators to plug in during shift changes or scheduled breaks, reducing the time the truck spends off the haul road solely to recharge. Overhead charging,   downhill recovery The NTE240E can also take power directly from overhead lines on equipped stretches of a haul road. Current collectors on the truck make contact with the lines, supplying electricity as the vehicle climbs with a load. Drawing power from the mine’s electrical infrastructure on uphill sections reduces how much energy the truck needs to take from its battery during the climb. On the descent, regenerative braking lets the truck recover some of the energy it would otherwise lose as heat. Its electric motors act as generators while slowing the vehicle, sending electricity back to the battery . NHL says the combination of onboard storage, overhead power and energy recovery makes the NTE240E 15 percent more energy-efficient than the ultra-class haul truck industry average. Lower costs than diesel NHL estimates the electric truck could cut operating costs by more than 60 percent compared with a similarly capable diesel hauler. It also projects that each truck could reduce carbon emissions by more than 2,000 tons a year. The battery-electric drivetrain eliminates the diesel engine and its associated generator, removing the need to service and overhaul those components. The economics will depend in part on how an individual mine is set up. An overhead line can supply power only on the sections it serves, and the dual-plug charging stop requires a site equipped to deliver power through both connections. The layout of the haul roads also determines how often a truck can use overhead power and how much energy it can recover on the return trip. For operators weighing a switch from diesel, those details will help determine how much time the truck can spend hauling between stops and how closely its running costs match NHL’s estimates.

title: New space armor takes 16,100-mph debris hits to protect astronauts
content: Space debris can strike spacecraft at speeds exceeding 16,000 mph, posing a serious threat to astronauts during spacewalks. Atomic-6 is investigating whether its satellite shielding technology could offer additional protection against these high-speed impacts.The company’s Space Armor® composite shield recently underwent testing at Texas A&M University’s Hypervelocity Impact Laboratory. A simulated torso behind the material showed no visible damage after a projectile struck at approximately 16,100 mph.A comparison using a solid aluminum plate produced a different outcome. Fragments became embedded in the simulated torso, demonstrating another hazard associated with high-speed impacts.Testing at extreme speedsEngineers fired a 3-millimeter aluminum sphere at two shielding configurations. The projectile traveled at approximately 7.2 kilometers per second, equivalent to 16,100 mph.Atomic-6 first placed a hexagonal Space Armor® Lite tile ahead of a transparent ballistic torso. Georgia-based Ballistic Dummy Lab supplied the model, which contained simulated soft tissue and skeletal structures.Post-impact inspections revealed no visible penetration or damage to the torso. The composite tile also showed no apparent cracking or bulging along its rear surface. For comparison, engineers substituted a 4-millimeter-thick solid aluminum plate. Both configurations maintained identical impact angles, spacing, and mounting arrangements.The aluminum plate produced fragments that became embedded in the simulated torso. This demonstrated a phenomenon known as rear-face spalling. Spalling occurs when an incoming projectile causes material to break away from a shield’s rear surface. Those fragments can travel toward the person or equipment behind it.Atomic-6 selected the aluminum plate’s thickness using NASA ballistic-limit equations. Engineers use these calculations to estimate whether shielding can withstand projectiles of particular sizes and speeds.The experiment did not compare complete spacesuits or traditional Whipple shields. The latter use separated bumper and rear-wall layers to disperse incoming debris.Could astronauts wear it?Space Armor® was originally developed to protect satellites against micrometeoroids and orbital debris (MMOD). Atomic-6 is now exploring whether its modular composite tiles could also protect astronauts during spacewalks.The Space Armor® Lite tile weighs approximately 31 pounds per square meter (14 kilograms per square meter). Its potential use in spacesuits will require considerable additional engineering.Former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield, an Atomic-6 advisory board member, described the initial findings as encouraging. He noted that orbital debris remains a persistent concern during spacewalks.Atomic-6 CEO Trevor Smith also sees astronaut protection as a potential extension of the technology. The company originally designed Space Armor® to shield spacecraft from high-speed debris.Significant challenges remain before the material could enter spacesuit development. Researchers used a stationary ballistic torso without a functioning spacesuit, pressure garment, or life-support equipment.Consequently, the experiment cannot establish whether the material prevents injuries or maintains suit pressure during an actual impact. Its performance under real space conditions also remains unknown.Atomic-6 plans additional experiments involving curved shields and different impact angles. These configurations should better represent an astronaut’s chest or shoulder.Engineers must also examine attachment systems, mobility, and pressure retention. Thermal-vacuum testing will be necessary to evaluate a potential spacesuit application.Space Armor® recently completed its first spaceflight aboard Portal Space Systems’ Starburst-1 spacecraft. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carried it during the Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission last month.That flight marked a milestone for the satellite shielding technology. Its potential role in astronaut protection will depend on the results of further testing.

title: World's first certified BESS made with used EV batteries, unveiled
content: The first certified battery energy storage system (BESS) made from second-life EV batteries, which comes with 500-kilowatt-hours (kWh) of energy storage capacity, has entered production in North America. Dubbed Nova, the system was developed by Moment Energy, a battery tech firm based in Canada. It is the world’s first BESS made from repurposed EV batteries to secure both UL 1973 and UL 9540 safety certifications.Moment Energy said that the BESS is intended for both commercial and industrial facilities. These could include hospitals, airports, and production sites. It can store electricity, cut energy costs, and even provide backup power during grid outages.Nova is already in production at the company’s Megafactory 1, the world’s largest EV battery repurposing plant, which is located in Surrey, British Columbia. The first deliveries are scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. Inside the storage systemAs per Moment Energy, each Nova block delivers 200 kilowatts (kW) of power and stores 500 kWh of electricity. It occupies a footprint of about 9.65 by 5.9 feet (2.94 by 1.80 meters), which makes it suitable for facilities with limited space. Moreover, multiple blocks can also be combined to create larger installations with storage capacities reaching tens of megawatt-hours (MWh). In addition, the BESS can use batteries from different types of electric vehicles. It relies on AI to monitor their condition and adjust their performance. Nova, Moment Energy’s next-gen battery energy storage system (BESS).Credit: Moment EnergyThis, according to the company, is especially important because used EV batteries can have different levels of remaining capacity after years of service. Meanwhile, it also comes with replaceable battery packs. The old batteries can be swapped out without replacing the entire storage unit or disturbing its concrete foundation.Gurmesh Sidhu, Moment Energy’s co-founder and CPO, also remarked that this could keep Nova running for more than 20 years. “With Nova, we’ve solved the engineering challenges that have prevented BESS made with EV batteries from scaling commercially,” Sidhu explained. Certified for commercial useNova has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications, which cover battery safety and complete energy storage systems, respectively. It has also undergone testing under UL 9540A, which evaluates how fires caused by overheating batteries could spread through an energy storage installation.“Repurposing electric vehicle batteries for stationary energy storage creates new technical considerations that must be carefully evaluated,” Jeff Smidt, senior vice president at UL Solutions, said in a press release. “UL Certification demonstrates that the evaluated battery and energy storage system met applicable safety requirements.”For extra protection, it uses liquid cooling, smoke and heat detectors, as well as flammable gas detection, and an integrated explosion prevention system. It can operate in temperatures ranging from -13 to 122 degrees Fahrenheit (-25 to 50 degrees Celsius) and at altitudes of up to 6,562 feet (2,000 meters).Moment Energy manufactures Nova in North America with batteries that have hit the end of their useful life in electric vehicles but still retain capacity for stationary storage. The company believes this could reduce the dependence on imported batteries and keep them in use for a longer period of time. Nova is currently available for orders. Commercial deliveries are set to begin in early 2027.

title: New Pentagon files reveal 1953 sighting of dark, elliptical UFO
content: The US Department of War has released a 1953 report detailing a dark, elongated elliptical object spotted by legendary Lockheed engineer Clarence “Kelly” Johnson and military flight-test personnel in California.The account is part of the eighth tranche of previously classified and historical unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) records published on November 20 under the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE).The report, identified as DOW-UAP-D206, compiles witness statements, sketches, and correspondence concerning a December 16, 1953, sighting near Agoura and Point Mugu in Southern California.Johnson and other witnesses described an unusual dark object with an elongated, elliptical appearance. Personnel aboard a Lockheed WV-2 aircraft also reported observing the phenomenon while flying over the coast.The Air Force’s Air Technical Intelligence Center (ATIC) eventually classified the sighting as a lenticular cloud. However, witness accounts questioned that explanation, describing the object’s apparent movement and sharply defined edges.The report does not include radar data, photographs or physical evidence that could establish the object’s identity. Its release nevertheless provides a more complete historical record of an unusual observation involving experienced aerospace personnel.Files span decadesThe latest release contains 43 records, comprising 40 documents and three videos from the Department of War and the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).Among the historical material are six CIA documents from 1952 examining flying-saucer reports and their potential national security implications. Some discuss the possibility of convening a panel of scientists to assess available evidence.The release also includes Air Force intelligence reports from 1957, several Project Blue Book case records, and documents concerning the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP) and its associated contractor work.Three videos submitted by US Central Command also feature in the latest batch. The footage includes infrared sensor recordings from military platforms in the Middle East, with the cases remaining unresolved.Another notable inclusion is a 2009 report prepared by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) under a Defense Intelligence Agency contract. The document discusses investigations into reported anomalous activity, including work associated with Utah’s Skinwalker Ranch.More records to followThe eighth release brings the total number of records published under PURSUE to 521, according to the program’s public archive.President Donald Trump announced the initiative in February, directing the Department of War and other federal agencies to identify and release government records concerning extraterrestrial life, UFOs and UAP.The first tranche appeared on May 8, with subsequent releases adding historical reports, military footage and intelligence documents.The Department of War has confirmed that another batch of records is already in preparation. Assistant to the Secretary of War for Public Affairs and Pentagon Chief Spokesman Sean Parnell said the department and its agency partners were actively working on the next release.“The Department of War and our agency partners are actively working on the next release of UAP files,” Parnell said in a statement.The department said the eighth tranche would remain accessible through its official PURSUE archive at WAR.GOV/UFO, with additional documents to be published on a rolling basis. It did not specify when the next batch would be released or how many records it would contain.The department describes the published materials as unresolved cases in which available evidence has not allowed officials to reach a definitive conclusion about the observed phenomena.

title: President Trump threatens massive taxes on overseas data centers
content: U.S. technology companies could face steep financial penalties if they build artificial intelligence data centers outside the country. President Donald Trump announced the threat Friday, arguing that overseas construction could give China greater access to critical computing infrastructure.Speaking during a White House press briefing, Trump said his administration would impose substantial penalties on companies pursuing such projects. He did not outline a specific tax structure or explain how officials would enforce the proposed restrictions. Trump also acknowledged that he had not discussed the plan with his administration.The warning adds another dimension to Washington’s efforts to maintain America’s technological advantage over China. It also raises questions about how U.S. technology companies will approach their increasingly international infrastructure investments.Trump wants infrastructure at homeTrump argued that American companies should prioritize domestic construction instead of expanding their data center operations overseas. He suggested that communities should welcome these facilities while negotiating financial benefits with developers.“You ought to take advantage of the data centers,” Trump said. He encouraged local officials to secure payments for their communities instead of blocking construction projects.His remarks reflect an administration that wants to accelerate domestic computing infrastructure. However, opposition from American communities has complicated that ambition.Large data centers require substantial electricity and supporting infrastructure. Their construction can also place additional pressure on local power networks. Residents have increasingly questioned whether the economic benefits justify these demands.The growing resistance has forced technology companies to reconsider how they approach potential host communities. Several industry leaders now promise greater transparency and stronger financial commitments.Tech giants face local oppositionGoogle and Meta have acknowledged growing mistrust surrounding data center construction. Executives from both companies told The Associated Press they are working to improve communication with communities.Technology companies have also offered financial incentives to secure local support. Some developers promise fewer taxpayer subsidies and greater contributions toward community infrastructure.Environmental commitments have become another important part of these negotiations. Companies are attempting to address concerns about resource consumption while defending data centers’ economic importance.The political consequences extend beyond individual construction projects. Opposition to large facilities became an important issue during the midterm election campaign. Rising electricity prices also fueled criticism of the industry’s expanding infrastructure requirements.Democratic candidates capitalized on those concerns by promising stronger oversight of energy-intensive developments. Local resistance has also created permitting obstacles for companies seeking construction approvals.Congress targets energy infrastructureWashington is simultaneously pursuing legislation that could accelerate domestic infrastructure development. The Republican-led Senate approved bipartisan permitting reform legislation Thursday. The proposal now moves to the House of Representatives.The legislation seeks to shorten reviews for power plants, transmission lines and other major energy projects. These changes could help developers address the electricity requirements of expanding data center networks.Importantly, the proposal also seeks to ensure data center operators cover their electricity consumption. Developers would also contribute toward improvements to the wider transmission network.Trump praised the Senate legislation, predicting substantial construction activity if it becomes law. His administration has also tightened restrictions on remote access to advanced American computing chips and servers.Those restrictions target China’s ability to obtain American technology for training advanced artificial intelligence models. Together, these policies reflect Washington’s broader effort to strengthen domestic computing capacity.

title: 10,000-ton US plant to make rare-earth-free permanent magnets at scale
content: Minnesota-based Niron Magnetics has announced plans to invest $1.8 billion in a new manufacturing campus in Alabama that will produce 10,000 metric tons of rare-earth-free permanent magnets annually, a move aimed at strengthening the U.S. supply chain for electric vehicles, consumer electronics, industrial equipment, and defense applications.The company said the facility will be built on a 1.6-million-square-foot campus in Dothan, Alabama, creating about 700 jobs. Construction is expected to begin in 2028, with commercial production targeted for 2029, according to a company announcement released Thursday, November 19.Once operational, the site will become one of the largest facilities dedicated to manufacturing permanent magnets without relying on rare-earth elements, which currently dominate the global magnet market.Scaling rare-earth-free magnet productionNiron said the Alabama plant will manufacture permanent magnets based on its Clean Earth Magnet technology, which uses iron nitride instead of conventional rare-earth materials such as neodymium and dysprosium.The company describes the technology as the world’s first high-performance permanent magnet platform that does not require rare-earth elements. However, the announcement did not include independent performance data or direct comparisons with conventional rare-earth magnets.Permanent magnets are critical components in electric motors, wind turbines, robotics, data centers, consumer electronics, and defense systems. Today, roughly 90 percent of global rare-earth permanent magnet production is concentrated overseas, creating supply-chain concerns for manufacturers in the United States and Europe.By replacing rare-earth elements with abundant materials such as iron and nitrogen, Niron aims to reduce dependence on imported critical minerals while expanding domestic manufacturing capacity.Expansion follows Minnesota facilityThe Alabama announcement builds on the company’s first commercial-scale manufacturing facility in Sartell, Minnesota, which is currently under construction.That plant is expected to begin production in 2027 with an annual manufacturing capacity of up to 1,500 metric tons. The larger Alabama campus would increase Niron’s production capacity by more than six times, marking a significant step toward high-volume commercial manufacturing.According to the company, the new facility is intended to support growing demand from industries seeking alternatives to conventional rare-earth magnets while strengthening domestic production of strategic components.Growing demand from AI, electrificationDemand for permanent magnets continues to rise as electric vehicles, industrial automation, renewable energy systems, robotics, and artificial intelligence infrastructure require increasingly efficient electric motors and actuators.Manufacturers have also sought to diversify supply chains amid geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over access to critical minerals used in conventional permanent magnets.Niron said its iron nitride magnets are designed to offer a rare-earth-free alternative for these applications while enabling industrial-scale production.The company did not disclose which customers will be supplied from the Alabama facility, nor did it provide production timelines beyond the planned 2028 construction start and 2029 production target.If completed as scheduled, the Dothan campus would become the company’s flagship manufacturing site and one of the largest U.S. facilities dedicated to producing permanent magnets without rare-earth materials.“The demand for permanent magnets is accelerating across industries ranging from electric vehicles to AI infrastructure,” the company said, adding that the Alabama investment is intended to establish a large-scale domestic manufacturing base for next-generation magnet technology.

title: 500 MWe reactor paired with nuclear fuel-recycling tech in new deal
content: The global energy sector faces a twin crisis: surging electricity demand from artificial intelligence and a looming shortage of mined uranium. Nuclear technology firm Nuclea Energy plans to tackle both problems using radioactive waste.Nuclea has finalized the purchase of key technologies and intellectual property from Moltex Energy Limited. The transaction, executed through its subsidiary Nuclea Energy Canada, clears a major condition for Nuclea’s upcoming stock market debut.Before going public, Nuclea must finalize its $350 million business combination with NorthStrive Acquisition Corp I. That valuation remains subject to standard closing adjustments, alongside NSAI shareholder approval, Form S-4 registration effectiveness, and a $3 million minimum cash requirement. Once listed, the merged company will hold a portfolio protected by more than 80 granted patents.Until now, Nuclea’s business centered on its Morpheus microreactor, a 3.5 to 50 MWe lead-cooled unit built to supply off-grid power for remote communities, defense installations, and mining sites. Acquiring Moltex’s assets expands Nuclea into large-scale grid power and creates a closed fuel loop where radioactive waste generates new electricity.Avoiding high-pressure containment vesselsCentral to this expansion is the Stable Salt Reactor Wasteburner (SSR-W), a 300 to 500 MWe fast-spectrum molten salt reactor built for continuous grid supply. Unlike conventional pressurized water reactors, the SSR-W runs at atmospheric pressure with liquid fuel salts sealed inside standard assemblies.This architecture avoids high-pressure containment vessels and reduces complex safety engineering. Regulators have already cleared the design through Phase 1 of the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission’s Vendor Design Review.To feed the reactor, Nuclea acquired the Waste To Stable Salt (WATSS) recycling process, which researchers have successfully tested on real spent fuel at Canadian Nuclear Laboratories. Using a non-aqueous pyrochemical method, WATSS extracts over 90% of transuranic elements from used CANDU reactor fuel and converts them into liquid chloride salt.This process shrinks the volume of high-level waste requiring deep underground burial by up to 95%. Because WATSS extracts actinides together rather than isolating pure plutonium, it eliminates the weapons-proliferation risks tied to traditional reprocessing.Market demand and commercial outlookThe market need for these technologies is growing rapidly. Power infrastructure draws up to $2 trillion in annual capital investment, yet the International Energy Agency expects global electricity demand to climb 3.1% a year through 2040.Simultaneously, the World Nuclear Association warns that output from existing uranium mines will drop by roughly half between 2030 and 2040. Meanwhile, the United States alone holds over 95,000 metric tons of spent fuel across 79 sites—a federal liability projected to cost nearly $62 billion by 2030.Chief Executive Josef Freundorfer noted that bringing fuel recycling and fast-spectrum reactors in-house transforms Nuclea beyond a microreactor developer. Executive Chairman and Co-Founder Sagar Sanghera added that the company will now collaborate with governments, utilities, and Indigenous communities to bring the technology to market.

title: Scientists overcome barrier to unlock metallic conductivity in MOFs
content: Turns out we know very little about the world of materials. In a recent development, a Taiwan-based team has designed a crystalline copper–sulfur metal–organic framework (MOF). And this material has triple power: it achieves rare metallic conductivity, exhibits strong infrared photoresponse, and half-metallic spin behavior.Scientists have long faced a tough choice between metals, which conduct electricity well but are hard be customize. Metal-organic frameworks offer flexible molecular design but act as electrical insulators. Researchers overcame this limitation by synthesizing a new copper-based crystalline framework. This material merges metallic conductivity with the tunable chemistry of a molecular lattice.It opens up several high-impact applications across electronics, sensing, and energy. Metallic conductivityNormally, customizable frameworks block electricity, and metals can’t be easily tweaked at the molecular level. This crystal gives scientists both in one material, plus two big bonuses. The study introduces a single-crystal MOF built from self-assembled copper-sulfur chains that allow electrons to glide smoothly across the crystal structure. Single-crystal device testing demonstrated an unusually high electrical conductivity of up to 120 siemens per centimeter for a crystalline metal-organic framework. Temperature-dependent measurements further verified zero activation energy, proving that the material supports genuine metallic charge transport.The crystals proved equally impressive when exposed to light. When exposed to infrared light, the crystal converts faint optical signals into a remarkably strong electrical current, reaching a responsivity of 8,100 amperes per watt. Long carrier lifetimes keep electrical charges moving before they fade away, allowing the sensor to capture even weak light signals with high accuracy. A wide linear dynamic range also ensures the material responds reliably across both dim and bright infrared conditions.These traits position the crystal as a compelling candidate for high-speed infrared sensors, energy storage systems, and next-generation optoelectronic hardware. It could help advance night-vision cameras, medical imaging, and high-speed optical communication.Copper atoms (pink) and sulfur atoms (yellow) form repeating zigzag chains in the crystal. Credit: Advanced Science (2026).Future applications Quantum-mechanical simulations revealed an even deeper surprise hidden inside the lattice.Theoretical modeling showed that the material enters an exotic half-metallic state, splitting electron behavior along spin lines. “This work redefines the understanding of MOF conductivity by establishing spin as a key quantum descriptor of electronic transport,” said co-corresponding author Dr. Michitoshi Hayashi, a research fellow at the Center for Condensed Matter Sciences at National Taiwan University.Spintronics relies on controlling both electron spin and electrical charge to enable faster, more energy-efficient memory and logic devices. Chemists could now use this new copper-sulfur framework to design and build such quantum electronic properties from the ground up.Its spin-selective conductivity makes it ideal for faster, lower-power spintronic memory, logic circuits, and quantum computing hardware. Exceptional infrared sensitivity also positions the crystal for high-speed photodetectors, night-vision imaging, autonomous vehicle LiDAR, and optical communications. Furthermore, its high electrical conductivity and thermal stability support advanced chemical sensors, supercapacitors, batteries, and light-driven energy conversion systems.The study was published in Advanced Science.

title: Claude helped prove 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, researcher claims
content: An Anthropic mathematician claims he has solved one of mathematics’ most difficult problems with help from Claude. Levent Alpöge announced the proposed proof on Friday, November 20, potentially bringing a 167-year mathematical mystery closer to resolution.The claim concerns the Riemann hypothesis, a foundational conjecture about the distribution of prime numbers. Alpöge says his work goes further, establishing the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH). However, independent mathematicians must still examine the proof before anyone can declare the problem solved.Claude’s mathematical breakthroughAlpöge published a four-page explanation alongside an extensive collection of Lean verification files. The archive reportedly contains approximately 239 megabytes of data and 175,187 source files.Lean is a formal proof assistant that checks mathematical arguments against established logical rules. Its verification system allows researchers to examine whether each step follows from the preceding assumptions.In his explanation, Alpöge credited Claude with making rapid progress during the final stages. He described an approach involving weighted prime sums, known as von Mangoldt sums. The proposed method also uses mathematical constructions called theta lifts.The mathematician acknowledged the emotional significance of potentially resolving such an influential problem. He described the development as losing a guiding light for mathematical research. However, he also expressed excitement about the scientific possibilities ahead.Why verification still mattersA Lean archive offers stronger evidence than an ordinary AI-generated mathematical explanation. However, compiling the code does not automatically establish that the intended conjecture has been proven.An independent verification project has reportedly confirmed that the downloaded files match Alpöge’s published archive. Its initial checks also found that the main theorem statements compile against Mathlib, Lean’s standard mathematics library.However, researchers must still examine the complete proof. They need to establish that the code addresses the conventional Riemann hypothesis. They must also check its mathematical definitions and identify any unsupported assumptions.The distinction matters because Alpöge claims to have proved the generalized version. GRH extends the original conjecture to related mathematical functions called Dirichlet L-functions.Million-dollar mathematical prizeGerman mathematician Bernhard Riemann introduced his original hypothesis in 1859. It proposes that every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function lies on a specific vertical line. That line has a real component of exactly one-half.The conjecture connects prime number distribution with the behavior of this complex mathematical function. Its implications reach across number theory, including results that researchers have established conditionally.The Clay Mathematics Institute recognizes the Riemann hypothesis as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems. Each carries a $1 million award.However, Alpöge’s announcement does not qualify for immediate prize consideration. Clay requires publication in an approved peer-reviewed outlet. The proposed solution must then survive at least two years of scrutiny and gain broad mathematical acceptance.If independent researchers validate the proof, Claude’s contribution could mark a defining moment in computational mathematics. Until then, the 167-year-old problem remains officially unsolved.

title: US ally tests robotic mule made from automotive and tank parts
content: The French Army has begun field trials of a new load-carrying unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) designed to haul heavy equipment and support battlefield maintenance crews without exposing soldiers to hostile fire. Handed over to the army’s Maintenance Brigade during Exercise DOUMENC in November 2026, the robotic mule represents the first of three vehicles slated for rapid evaluation.Developed in just one year through a partnership between Franco-German defense contractor KNDS and French automotive supplier FORVIA, the platform reflects a broader push by France’s armed forces to accelerate adoption of ground robotics. Rather than spending years perfecting a fully autonomous system before putting hardware in the field, military engineers are deploying the vehicle in stages so troops can train alongside unmanned machines immediately.Three-tier autonomy According to the French Army Technical Section, known by its French initials STAT, the initial evaluation took place during Exercise DOUMENC from November 7 to 11, 2026, in coordination with the Direction Générale de l’Armement (DGA) and the Logistics Brigade. Equipped with an open mesh cargo flatbed, the wheeled UGV is built to haul crates of spare parts, tools, and infantry gear across rugged terrain. The program is structured around three progressive levels of control. At the baseline tier, soldiers operate the vehicle directly using a handheld remote controller. At the second level, an integrated robotization kit allows a remote operator to steer the mule from a safe distance using live onboard camera feeds. At the third tier, the UGV navigates autonomously within operational boundaries defined by the KNDS and FORVIA system architecture.STAT described the trial as “a first concrete step” toward ground robotics that everyday soldiers can operate routinely. By gradually scaling from manual teleoperation to bounded autonomy, the army aims to reduce the physical load carried by troops while shielding mechanics and resupply teams from direct enemy fire.Civil tech drives defense roboticsThe pairing of KNDS and FORVIA highlights how European defense planners are tapping commercial automotive manufacturing to shorten development cycles. While KNDS brings heavy military vehicle engineering and combat robotics experience, having previously converted a legacy AMX-30 main battle tank into a remote-controlled platform using its TOXO robotization kit, FORVIA contributes high-volume automotive electronics, sensors, and chassis integration.Exercise DOUMENC itself carries symbolic weight for French military logistics. Named after Captain Aimé Doumenc, who organized motorized supply convoys along the Voie Sacrée during the 1916 Battle of Verdun, the 2026 drill serves as France’s national evaluation ground for modernizing combat sustainment.Toward unmanned ground fleetFrance’s army leadership has set a long-term goal of fielding battle-ready robotic units by 2040, with logistics and load-carrying mules serving as the practical entry point before armed ground systems enter service. Alongside the KNDS-FORVIA mule, STAT and French regiments have tested multiple unmanned platforms throughout 2026, including the hydrogen-powered Hermione UGV and compact forward-reconnaissance rovers. Two additional KNDS-FORVIA vehicles will join the Maintenance Brigade in upcoming trials to refine autonomous navigation and payload handling under realistic field conditions.

title: 100,000-ton-capacity pure hydrogen pipeline enters service in China
政策分类路径: 政策 > 战略规划型政策 > 产业方向
政策分类依据: 国家能源局将该项目列为首批氢能试点，体现国家氢能产业战略方向与碳达峰碳中和目标规划
content: China’s first pure hydrogen pipeline transporting green hydrogen over more than 62 miles (100 km) has entered service in the industrial city of Baotou in north China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.The 121-mile (195-km) pipeline is expected to significantly lower the cost of moving hydrogen from production sites to industrial users, with transportation costs projected to fall by about 77 percent once the project reaches its designed capacity.According to the state news agency, the National Energy Administration selected the project as one of the country’s first hydrogen-energy pilot projects. The start of operations was announced during the 2026 Hydrogen Energy Industry Development Conference held in Baotou on Thursday, November 19.Wind, solar farms power green hydrogen productionThe pipeline transports green hydrogen from a production facility in Darhan Muminggan United Banner to industrial customers in Baotou. It currently supports an annual green hydrogen production capacity of about 7,800 tonnes, marking an important step toward building dedicated hydrogen infrastructure for China’s growing clean-energy sector.The project also takes advantage of Inner Mongolia’s abundant renewable energy resources. Large-scale wind and solar farms in the region generate the electricity needed to produce green hydrogen through water electrolysis. According to Baotou Mayor Meng Qingwei, the fuel will help decarbonize established industrial sectors, including chemical manufacturing, metallurgy, industrial gases, and transportation.“This will help expand the use of green hydrogen in chemicals, metallurgy, and transportation, while providing valuable experience for the construction and operation of large-scale pure hydrogen pipelines,” said Wang Xinyu, a director of project developer Inner Mongolia Huadian Hydrogen Energy Industry Technology Development Co., Ltd.Although the pipeline has only begun supplying hydrogen, it was designed with considerable room for expansion. At full capacity, it will be able to transport up to 100,000 tonnes of hydrogen annually. Project officials estimate that the cost of transporting green hydrogen could fall from around $1.94 per kilogram to approximately $0.45 per kilogram, pegging a reduction of about 77 percent. Authorities, however, have not indicated when the pipeline is expected to reach its maximum operating capacity.Overcomes transport bottlenecks The project also addresses one of the biggest challenges facing the emerging hydrogen economy: transportation. As countries around the world accelerate efforts to decarbonize heavy industry and diversify their energy systems, hydrogen has become an increasingly important part of long-term energy strategies. Yet moving the gas efficiently remains difficult. Transporting hydrogen by road using tube trailers is expensive and limited in volume, while dedicated pipelines require specialized materials and engineering to handle the fuel safely.Unlike natural gas, hydrogen molecules are extremely small and can diffuse into steel, causing a phenomenon known as hydrogen embrittlement that can weaken pipelines operating under high pressure.To overcome this challenge, Baotou Iron and Steel Group developed specialized anti-hydrogen-embrittlement steel specifically for the project. Engineers also tackled a series of construction challenges, including difficult geological conditions, mountainous terrain, and the demanding welding and corrosion-protection requirements associated with high-pressure hydrogen pipelines.The completion of the pipeline also aligns with China’s broader hydrogen ambitions. According to official figures, the country produced more than 39 million tonnes of hydrogen in 2025, making it the world’s largest producer and consumer of the fuel.China outlined its long-term hydrogen strategy in 2022 through the National Hydrogen Energy Development Plan (2021-2035). The plan aims to establish an orderly nationwide hydrogen industry by 2030 while accelerating the production and use of renewable hydrogen to help meet the country’s carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals.Infrastructure projects such as the Baotou pipeline are expected to play an important role in connecting renewable hydrogen production with industrial demand, reducing costs, and supporting wider commercial adoption across multiple sectors.

title: Rare p-wave magnetism observed in simple metal, could boost quantum tech
content: An international collaboration of researchers from 19 institutions across the world has found experimental evidence for p-wave magnetism in a chemically simple metallic compound, europium silicide (EuSi). This could help researchers further explore how chirality and magnetic symmetry influence electronic properties and could open new areas of technology from spintronics to superconductivity. In a conventional ferromagnet, the electron spins align in the the same direction, which produces magnetization. P-wave magnetism is different since atomic spins arrange into a spiral or helical pattern, resulting in no magnetization. However, if the electron spins are split by the direction of motion, then it generates a p-wave magnetic pattern. In the p-wave state, electrons moving in opposite directions have opposite spin polarizations. This relationship between electron momentum and spin is called an odd-parity spin texture. The challenge of p-wave magnetism has been to find suitable materials with these properties. Previous attempts to understand this phenomenon included candidates with very low magnetic ordering temperatures or complicated symmetry. Why is EuSi special? EuSi can be grown as single crystals of high quality made from stoichiometric metal. This makes it ideal for systematic experiments. “What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal,” said Claudia Felser, director at MPI CPfS. Erjian Cheng, a researcher at the MPI CPfS in Dresden, Germany, grew high-quality crystals of EuSi around three years ago. Preliminary research on these crystals showed a strong influence of the magnetic order on their electronic band structure. “That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state,” explained Cheng in a press release. The researchers wondered if EuSi hosted an unconventional magnetic state and probed this further using neutron-scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy. How did scientists spot it? The team found that at temperatures between 33 and 62 Kelvin (-240 degrees Celsius and -211 degrees Celsius), magnetic moments of Europium atoms formed an ordered spiral. While these spins are substantial, they cancel each other, resulting in no net magnetization. In their p-wave state, the electrons moving in opposite directions had opposite spin polarizations. Spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy showed a characteristic sign change in electron spin polarization in regions where the p-wave spin texture vanishes, thereby indicating a p-wave magnetic state. Even though the crystal structure of EuSi is centrosymmetric or symmetric around a central point, the spiral arrangement of magnetic spins can give it a magnetic state of opposite handedness. “This demonstrates how the discovery of new materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties,” added Felser in the press release. Theory suggests that p-wave magnets made from metals show strong current-induced responses, unconventional superconducting states and spin-polarized electronic transport without an external magnetic field. Even though scientists have not yet attempted to demonstrate these effects in EuSi, the availability of the material makes it possible to verify the theory through laboratory experiments. It also shows that the properties of quantum materials is not defined by the chemical composition or structure but also by their symmetry and magnetic order. The research findings were published in the journal Nature.

title: Brain’s ‘3D GPS’ could guide next-gen brain-computer interfaces
content: Scientists in China have found a “3D GPS” in the motor cortex of macaques that tracks where the hand is as it moves. The researchers detected the signal by recording brain activity while the animals reached for objects, then used it to reconstruct the paths their hands took.The study was led by Yu Shan at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Automation. The team also found signals linked to where the macaques intended to grasp, a finding that could give brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) a more direct way to interpret reaching movements.How neurons map handThe researchers let the macaques choose when and where to reach. They recorded individual neurons with microelectrode arrays implanted in two areas on the left side of the brain. One, the primary motor cortex, helps execute movements. The other, the dorsal premotor cortex, helps plan them.About 36.2 percent of recorded neurons in the primary motor cortex responded to the hand’s position at any given moment. The figure was 21.3% in the dorsal premotor cortex.“These neurons do not simply increase or decrease their firing rates linearly with distance. Instead, they behave like localized ‘hotspots,’ becoming significantly more active when the hand enters a particular region of space,” the study’s first author Cao Shenghao said.Fewer neurons for mappingWhen the researchers reconstructed hand paths, position-sensitive cells making up just 17.7 percent of the recorded neurons in the dorsal premotor cortex achieved 94.1 percent of the decoding performance of the full group.In the primary motor cortex, a subset comprising 32.8 percent of recorded neurons reached 92.9 percent of full-group performance.A further analysis estimated that 2.8 position-sensitive neurons in the dorsal premotor cortex and 16.4 in the primary motor cortex were sufficient, on average, to reach 90 percent of full-group performance.Those figures describe statistical averages from the experiment. An implant would still have to record enough usable signals to identify the relevant neurons.From macaque brains to human implantsSome motor BCIs estimate speed and direction before piecing together the path of a movement. Reading position signals directly could let a decoder skip some of those calculations.If the approach works in humans, a device could choose how to move a robotic limb once the interface identifies where the user wants it to go.Cao said the approach could eventually help people who have lost arm movement after strokes. Researchers still need human recordings to establish whether the same kinds of neurons represent hand position and grasp targets. They would also have to keep those signals usable over years of implantation. Signal quality can deteriorate, and the neural activity a decoder relies on can change over time.Cao said fine hand movements and reliable operation without recalibration remain beyond what the research demonstrates. The next question is whether the same signals can give a person with impaired movement reliable control of an external device in daily life, where reaching is often only the first step toward picking up and using an object.The study was recently published in the Journal of Neuroscience.

title: World’s largest electric cargo ship with 23.5 MWh battery set for maiden voyage
content: The world’s largest battery-powered bulk carrier has left China and is on its way to Norway, where it will be equipped with a massive 23.5-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery. The 426-foot (129.9-meter) ship, known as BRF Froan, was built by Jiangsu SOHO Marine Heavy Industry for Norwegian shipping firm Berge Rederi. It will transport marble along the Norwegian coast without burning fuel.“We are pleased to announce the successful registration of BRF Froan under the Norwegian flag,” the Norwegian Maritime Authority shared. “This latest addition further strengthens Norway’s position as an attractive and competitive flag state.”The vessel has a cargo capacity of 13,250 deadweight tonnes (DWT) and has two 79-foot (24-meter) rotor sails to slash electricity consumption. Once operational, it will significantly reduce carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions.Battery and rotor sailsFor propulsion, BRF Froan will rely on its battery system. Berge Rederi pointed out that charging facilities at both ends of its route will provide the electricity needed for each journey. The ship will travel approximately 230 nautical miles (265 miles) between Brønnøy and Elnesvågen. Berge Rederi explained that this is considerably longer than the 15-nautical-mile journey the Trøndelag-headquartered company currently identifies as the longest route operated by a battery-electric ferry. “Furthermore, the vessel will exemplify the extraordinary potential of achieving large-scale maritime operations with zero emissions,” Berge Rederi representatives added.The BRF Froan during construction.Credit: Berge RederiThe ship has two rotor sails. Each measures 79 feet (24 meters) tall and 13 feet (four meters) wide. These rotating cylinders use wind to generate additional thrust and reduce the amount of power required from the ship’s propulsion system.Berge Rederi estimates that the two sails will provide average power savings of 339 kilowatts (kW) per voyage. The vessel will also feature an electric excavator for cargo operations. Moreover, the company plans to install 10,764 square feet (1,000 square meters) of solar panels on the ship’s hatch covers.The shore charging facilities will consume 5.13 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually. “Shore power facilities will be installed in both ports, allowing the vessel to recharge the batteries,” the company said.Cleaner marble transportBRF Froan will operate under a five-year contract to transport over 14 US tons (up to 13,000 tonnes) of marble from Brønnøy and Visnes to Omya Hustadmarmor’s processing facility in Elnesvågen. The marble will then undergo processing to produce calcium carbonate, a material used in various industries.The project goal is to eliminate emissions during cargo transport and loading by using batteries, electric equipment, and electricity supplied from ports. Apart from reducing CO2 emissions by roughly 10,000 US tons (9,000 tonnes) annually, the vessel will prevent around 220 US tons (200 tonnes) of nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions each year.Artist’s rendering of the BRF Froan electric bulk carrier.Credit: Berge RederiThe total cost of the project is approximately USD 52 million (NOK 500 million). Around USD 28 million (NOK 270 million) comes from Norway’s Enova and NOx Fund. A second vessel, named BRF Frøya, is already under construction in China and is scheduled for delivery in 2027.The Norwegian Maritime Authority congratulated Berge Rederi Future AS on the successful delivery and registration of the vessel. “We are proud and grateful for your continued confidence in the Norwegian flag,” the agency shared. “We wish BRF Froan and her crew safe and successful voyages in the years ahead.”

title: US 'doomsday plane' trails Air Force One at 720 mph over Pacific
content: The US Air Force’s E-4B Nightwatch was spotted over the Pacific on Thursday as President Donald Trump flew home from China. Military flight tracker Andrew Leyden shared data showing the aircraft, a modified Boeing 747 nicknamed the “doomsday plane,” south of Japan after Trump attended the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.The Nightwatch was one of four Boeing 747s that trackers spotted on the return leg. The other three were presidential aircraft, including the jet carrying Trump. The E-4B gives the president and senior military leaders an airborne command post if they lose access to command centers on the ground.Four Boeing 747s on the return legLeyden wrote on X that “Air Force One and the two other 747 backup aircraft are currently over Japan, along with the E-4 Doomsday plane.” He added that Trump “was seen boarding the VC-25B in Shenzhen,” identifying the aircraft that was serving as Air Force One on the trip home.The US Air Force sent all three presidential 747s on the trip, Defence Blog reported. A screenshot from ADS-B Exchange that Leyden shared showed the Nightwatch flying at about 31,000 feet. It was moving northeast at about 720 mph over the ground, according to the same screenshot, which identified the aircraft by its call sign.Leyden said a C-32, the military version of the Boeing 757 commonly used to carry staff and reporters, had also flown on the trip but “is currently not on the trackers.”What the E-4B does in an emergencyThe Air Force modified the Boeing 747 so senior leaders could communicate with US forces from the air during a national emergency. That includes maintaining contact with US nuclear forces if military command facilities on the ground become unavailable.The aircraft “frequently shadows the US president on international trips for security reasons,” the South China Morning Post reported during Trump’s May visit to Beijing.The jets had separate destinations in the US. Air Force One was headed to Joint Base Andrews outside Washington, while the E-4B was returning to its home base at Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska.Russia’s nuclear briefcase appears in ShenzhenTrump met Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for three-way talks on Thursday. title: BAE Systems opens fully automated munitions plant for 155mm shells
content: BAE Systems has officially opened the United Kingdom’s first fully automated large-caliber munitions facility at its historic manufacturing complex in Glascoed, South Wales. Funded by a £180 million (roughly $228 million) investment, the new melt-cast explosive-filling plant is engineered to expand the defense contractor’s 155mm artillery shell production capacity sixteen-fold compared to 2023 output levels.The opening addresses a pressing industrial bottleneck across Western defense supply chains, where high-intensity artillery consumption in Ukraine has strained allied ammunition stockpiles. By replacing labor-intensive manual handling with industrial robotics and autonomous transport, the facility is designed to run extended production shifts while keeping human technicians outside volatile high-explosive zones.Inside automated facility According to a BAE Systems announcement on November 20, 2026, the plant relies on a coordinated network of industrial robotic systems and autonomous guided vehicles (AGVs) to move, position, and fill steel artillery casings without direct human intervention inside hazardous bays. Empty 155mm shell bodies machined at BAE Systems’ facility in Washington, northeast England, are transported south to Glascoed to receive their high-explosive payloads. At the core of the operation is an automated melt-cast process. During production, solid energetic compounds are carefully heated until liquefied, poured directly into the empty 155mm steel casings, and cooled under tightly controlled thermal profiles until solidified before moving on to final fuzing and assembly. Uniform solidification is critical in melt-cast munitions manufacturing because trapped air pockets, shrinkage voids, or hairline cracks inside the explosive core can cause erratic detonation or premature barrel failures when fired from high-pressure howitzers.“Glascoed has been at the center of the UK’s munitions capability for generations,” said Andrea Thompson, Group Managing Director of BAE Systems Digital Intelligence & Land. “By combining our extensive experience with advanced automation, we’re creating a facility that delivers significantly greater capacity, improves resilience of supply and supports the UK’s defense needs long into the future.”Delays, capacity upgrades, and UK supply resilienceSpread across a 1,000-acre (405-hectare) complex in Monmouthshire that has produced munitions since the 1940s, Glascoed employs roughly 870 staff and anchors Britain’s domestic energetics sector. The automated plant arrives more than a year after its originally targeted summer 2025 debut. According to reports, construction schedules were extended after BAE Systems made a strategic mid-project decision to double the plant’s planned capacity from an eightfold increase to sixteen-fold. A scale-up is expected to lift annual 155mm production from roughly 3,000 to 5,000 shells to around 80,000 rounds.The upgrade also fits into a much bigger modernization effort across Britain’s artillery supply chain. Alongside the Glascoed filling line and its shell-forging site in Washington, BAE Systems has reopened gun-barrel manufacturing in Sheffield and invested in continuous-flow processing for explosives and propellants to reduce British reliance on imported energetic materials from the United States and France. While the Glascoed facility is now officially open, full-scale mass production will ramp up following an initial phase of live safety and process qualification trials.

content:
Clarity Sensors to develop perovskite photon-counting detector for medical CT with £1.9M UK grant
Cambridge spin-out
Clarity Sensors
has been awarded a £1.9 million (about US$2.5 million) Product Development Award from the UK’s National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) to develop a perovskite-based photon-counting detector module for medical CT imaging. Clarity Sensors leads the three-year project, called PICASO, and receives £1.3 million (about US$1.7 million). The rest funds the work of the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) Technology Department. The project began on October 1, 2026.
Photon-counting CT measures the energy of individual X-ray photons, which gives higher-resolution images at a lower radiation dose than conventional CT. Wider adoption is held back by the sensor materials used today, cadmium telluride and cadmium zinc telluride. These take months to grow at temperatures above 750 °C, and only a few suppliers can make them at medical grade. As a result, photon-counting CT is mostly limited to specialist centers. Clarity Sensors is developing a second generation of sensor based on halide perovskite single crystals, which are grown at about 40 °C in days. The company says its sensors have performed comparably with the cadmium telluride sensors in current commercial systems on key detector measures in laboratory tests. It adds that they have operated stably under X-ray flux and bias conditions relevant to CT.
PICASO will pair these sensors with STFC’s HEXITECMHz readout electronics, which run at a continuous one million frames per second. The partners will optimize the readout chip for perovskite sensors, then build a complete detector module and validate it in a CT-relevant preclinical environment. The aim is to take the technology from Technology Readiness Level 3 to 6. Clarity Sensors will also set up pilot-scale sensor production at its Cambridge facility and implement ISO 13485 quality management controls.
Dr. Hayden Salway, CEO of Clarity Sensors and Lead Applicant, said: “Photon-counting CT offers real benefits for patients, but the materials it depends on today are slow and costly to make. We grow our perovskite sensors in a matter of days at low temperature, and our initial laboratory results show they can already perform comparably with the materials in current systems. This NIHR award, and our collaboration with STFC’s detector specialists, will allow us to turn these results into a complete detector module and test it under the conditions a CT scanner demands. It is a significant step towards our goal of supplying perovskite semiconductor detector technology to CT manufacturers.”
Dr. Matthew Veale, Group Leader of the STFC Technology Department’s Detector Development Group, added: “For 20 years, our HEXITEC® technology has advanced the field of colour X-ray imaging, bringing capabilities once confined to national science facilities into laboratories and industry. The combination of our next-generation HEXITECMHz detector technology with Clarity Sensors’ innovative perovskite semiconductor materials represents an exciting opportunity to widen access to affordable colour CT imaging. With NIHR funding, working with Clarity Sensors, we aim to advance knowledge of these emerging materials, improve lives through the development of more accessible medical imaging technologies, and drive growth by strengthening UK sovereign capability in advanced X-ray detector technologies.”
